# I0861 Dossier: China-Asset Diligence Desk for Pharma BD

Research date: 2026-10-13. Labels: **[F]** fact from a cited source, **[I]** my inference or model, **[G]** gap. Where sources disagree I say so.

## Bottom line

The problem is real and getting more acute, but it points to a **small, high-margin specialist boutique, not a venture-scale company**. Four findings drive that.

1. A direct competitor the prior pass missed already sells data-integrity and GCP audit-trail spot checks on China-originated assets (Vision Lifesciences, below).
2. Even at generous assumptions, the reachable annual revenue pool is roughly $1.5-4M [I].
3. The 72-hour promise depends on seller data access, which Chinese data rules and trust gaps constrain.
4. BIOSECURE is a weaker why-now than claimed; FDA and Congress scrutiny of China-site data is the stronger one.

Direct evidence that buyers pay for this exact service is thin [G]. Verdict: viable as a law-firm-channel red-flag memo plus seller-side readiness review. Not viable as a database or software play.

## 1. Market context and industry metrics

Industry-defining metrics: deals per year, upfront per deal, buyer segment mix, diligence cost per deal, and regulator acceptance rate for China-site data.

- **Deal count (sources conflict).** 186 Greater China out-licensing deals in 2025 per Pharmcube via [Reuters/Yahoo](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/analysis-china-biotech-licensing-boom-092338804.html). Evaluate counts a narrower set, 93 Western-China licensing deals in 2025, up from 42 in 2022, in [Fierce](https://www.fiercebiotech.com/biotech/analyst-china-no-longer-bargain-basement-biotech-acquisitions) (page returned 403; read via search summary). H1 2026: 81 deals per NMPA and 86 per Insight (+34% YoY), per [The Standard](https://www.thestandard.com.hk/finance/article/337073/China-innovative-drug-out-licensing-deal-value-reaches-new-high-in-first-half-of-2026-says-CCTV) and [IQVIA](https://www.iqvia.com/locations/emea/blogs/2026/07/biopharma-ma-mid-year-2026-update).
- **Value (sources conflict).** 2025 headline value was $135.7B per NMPA, cited in [Morgan Lewis](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/04/a-strategic-playbook-for-chinese-biotech-cross-border-deals-navigating-the-new-value-paradigm), and $137.7B per Pharmcube. Over $60B came in Q1 2026 alone. Headline value is mostly contingent: Pharmcube's H1 2026 upfronts were $4.97B, about 5% of headline.
- **Upfronts.** Evaluate's average upfront rose from $52M (2022) to $172M (early 2026), per [BioPharma APAC](https://biopharmaapac.com/analysis/71/8225/discount-or-validation-western-pharmas-appetite-for-chinese-assets.html). Reuters cites a different definition: $77.7M average in 2026 so far vs $38.8M in 2025. Only about 40 of roughly 92 deals disclosed an upfront, so averages are self-selected.
- **Share.** One-third of 2025 licensing spend involved China-sourced drugs per Jefferies, via [BioPharma Dive](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/china-biotech-drug-licensing-deals-pipeline/758283/) (secondary reporting; I did not find the Jefferies report itself). The idea file's two headline deals check out: [Lilly-InnoCare](https://pharmaphorum.com/news/lilly-forges-335bn-alliance-chinas-innocare) is up to $3.35B but is a discovery-platform collaboration with no asset package to verify. [Merck-SciBrunch](https://njbiz.com/merck-scibrunch-kras-cancer-drug-deal/) is $2.13B with $400M upfront for a **preclinical** KRAS G12D inhibitor. Preclinical packages are where GLP-tox and CMC verification matter most [I].
- **Scale of spend vs the sprint.** A $45k sprint is about 0.03-0.06% of the $78-172M average upfront [I]. Price is not the objection; trust and access are.

## 2. Competitors

| Player | What they sell | Funding / traction | Overlap |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Vision Lifesciences** (HK HQ; Shanghai, Zurich, Chicago) | "Three Pillars Diligence": data integrity and GCP audit trail with source-document spot checks; CMC tech-transfer audit; IP/FTO. [Page](https://visionlifesciences.com/insights/china-biotech-licensing-opportunities-2026) | No pricing, funding or named deals disclosed. Marketing page is internally inconsistent (says $135B "in 2026", ~$138B elsewhere). | **Direct on paper** |
| Alacrita | Pre-DD triage, full technical DD, and "DD Readiness" including checking presentations against source data. 14 core staff plus network. [Page](https://www.alacrita.com/our-services/due-diligence) | Private, undisclosed. No China-specific offer found. | Adjacent; has the seller-side product |
| Patsnap Synapse | AI drug-asset DD reports | Series E ~$300M, >$1B valuation ([IAM](https://www.iam-media.com/market-developments/asian-ip-analytics-unicorn-emerges-softbank-tencent-backing)); >$100M ARR claimed ([Vertex](https://www.vertexventures.sg/news/patsnap-surpasses-us-100-million-in-annual-recurring-revenue-reinforces-position-as-a-global-leader-in-ip-and-r-d-intelligence/)) | Adjacent; can add |
| Pharmcube | China deal/trial data and consulting | ~$15.6M raised, last round 2021 ([CB Insights](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/pharmcube/financials)) | Adjacent; small balance sheet |
| Banyan (Locust Walk) | NewCo builder, 5 staff in China, $100M+ commitments, 2-3 deals/yr, none announced yet. Its CEO says "getting data out of the company can be challenging." [PharmaVoice](https://www.pharmavoice.com/news/china-biotech-drug-investment-banyan-pharma-deal/825444/) | Funded | Customer or substitute |
| Perceptic | AI platform claiming to compress scientific DD "from weeks to hours" | $12M seed, Accel ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/05/26/exclusive-perceptic-a-startup-automating-drug-discovery-end-to-end-for-big-pharma-emerges-from-stealth-with-12-million-in-seed-funding/)); not China-specific | Substitute for the LLM-extraction layer |
| Redica | Inspection datasets | ~$57M raised ([CB Insights](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/redica-systems/financials)); Jan 2026 expansion covered Japan, Swiss, EMA, Korea, **not NMPA** ([Redica](https://www.redica.com/resources/post/redica-expands-global-inspection-coverage-with-new-pmda-swissmedic-ema-and-mfds-data)) | Data commodity, China gap may close |
| Interos / Kharon / Sayari | Supply-chain and list screening | Interos $40M ([Oct 2024](https://stocktitan.net/news/OWL/interos-secures-40m-investment-from-blue-owl-4dfm65jzp7je.html)) plus $20M ([Jan 2026](https://www.thesaasnews.com/news/interos-ai-bags-20-million-in-funding)); Kharon: only a Barclays seed found ([CB Insights](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/kharon/financials)); Sayari pitches [BIOSECURE screening](https://sayari.com/?p=20299) | Overlaps the "second product" |
| GCP audit vendors (e.g. [The FDA Group](https://www.thefdagroup.com/services/gcp-auditing)), CRO regulatory arms | Mock BIMO inspections, site/TMF audits | Established | Could repackage as in-licensing audits |

**Incumbents who could add this:** Patsnap and Pharmcube (data plus consulting), Norstella/Evaluate, ICON (already sells [technical DD covering tox, CMC, regulatory](https://iconplc.com/services/consulting/asset-development/due-diligence-asset-valuation)), PwC (publishes a [China-specific diligence framework](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/industries/health-industries/library/china-biotech-sector.html)), and law firms. RA Capital's Swiftbridge has already internalized the function for its portfolio (per prior research; Fierce page not retrievable).

**Positioning read:** Vision is the only player I found claiming spot checks of source documents on China packages, but I found no evidence of customers, price or scientist depth [G]. A boutique with named, FDA-experienced bilingual scientists can differentiate on credibility; it cannot claim white space. Big buyers verify in house and "have been able to pay closer to full value," while smaller buyers lose contested assets, per BioPharma APAC. That supports the target segment (below-scale buyers).

## 3. Bottom-up market size [I, modeled]

No source counts reachable buyers [G]. Model:

- Deal flow: 2026 run rate about 170-190 out-licensing deals (2 x 81-95 H1).
- Remove big pharma, which takes about 40% of assets in-licensed (IQVIA figure cited by Fierce) and runs its own teams, plus deals with no verifiable package. Assume 50-60% of deals sit with buyers lacking a China bench, giving **85-110 addressable transactions/year**.
- Attach rate for pre-signing independent verification: 15-25% (assumption, no source). That is 13-28 sprints x $25-70k (mid $45k), or **$0.6-1.3M**.
- Retainers: perhaps 15-25 NewCo or VC platforms are active buyers of China assets. Examples: K2 Therapeutics' [$50M seed](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/k2-ying-huang-biotech-startup-mpm-china-drugs/827544/), Banyan, plus Kailera and Verdiva-type vehicles. At 20-30% adoption x $150-300k, that is 3-6 retainers, or **$0.5-1.5M**.
- Add seller-side readiness reviews and post-signing tech-transfer checks: +$0.5-1M.
- **Realistic pool $1.5-4M/yr.** Even if every one of 186 deals bought a mid-priced sprint, the ceiling is about $8.4M.

New buyer type: Royalty Pharma opened a Hong Kong office and hired a head of Asia in 2026 ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/business/china-business/article/3358830/funding-option-royalties-giant-opens-hong-kong-base-mainland-china-biotech-deals-surge)), a plausible royalty-fund customer. But royalty funds underwrite late-stage assets, a thin slice.

## 4. Evidence of demand and willingness to pay

**Pain evidence (moderate to strong):**
- BioPharma APAC: diligence on China-origin assets is "harder and more expensive for a buyer without people on the ground," and part of the upfront discount is a diligence-cost discount. That is a price signal for verification.
- The [BioWorld](https://www.bioworld.com/articles/733985-asian-data-face-global-test-in-biotech-deals) Asia Bio Partnering Forum panel (Sep 2026): data packages must withstand partner diligence, regulators and cross-border transfer rules.
- Morgan Lewis: MNCs demand validation that Chinese data meets FDA/EMA standards and scrutinize licensor data-transfer compliance.
- Failures: Novo Nordisk alleges KBP withheld negative data and concealed site compliance problems in a deal worth up to $1.3B, seeks about $830M, and won an asset freeze upheld in Singapore, with arbitration pending ([pharmaphorum](https://pharmaphorum.com/news/novo-nordisk-fight-kbp-bio-will-go-arbitration), allegations unadjudicated). Elevar's rivoceranib got a CRL over GMP deficiencies at partner Hengrui's facility and incomplete BIMO inspections ([Patsnap news](https://synapse.patsnap.com/news-detail/99578c96-ea2b-3216-a213-b60072390ed8-elevar-to-resubmit-liver-cancer-drug-to-fda)). A 72-hour paper review would likely catch an Elevar-type facility-history gap but not a KBP-type concealment [I].

**Willingness-to-pay evidence (weak):**
- No RFP, price list or buyer budget line found [G]. Competitors publish no prices.
- Adjacent spend is large: Lepu paid a BD consultant a $500,000 retainer (plus disputed success fees) in a [suit reported by Fierce](https://fiercebiotech.com/biotech/pioneer-china-newco-model-sued-over-trade-secret-misuse-double-dealing) (allegations only). Buyers and sellers do pay heavily for China deal access, but that is sell-side BD, not verification.
- Counter-evidence: RA Capital and Banyan are internalizing; Pfizer's CEO publicly discussed scrutinizing Chinese data in house (per a PwC-linked [Fierce](https://fiercebiotech.com/biotech/chinas-rapid-rise-creates-heightened-risks-pharma-pwc) item; I could not confirm details).

## 5. Unit economics [I]

- Sprint staffing: 2 bilingual scientists x about 50 hours, 1 principal reviewer x 15 hours, 10 hours of coordination and tooling. Benchmark rates from an [NIH-hosted guide](https://seed.nih.gov/sites/default/files/2024-12/Regulatory-and-Manufacturing-Consulting-for-Life-Sciences.pdf): $100-200/hr junior, $600-1,000+/hr principal.
- Fully loaded delivery cost is about $20-35k per sprint, so margin runs roughly 0-30% at the $25k floor and 50-70% at $70k. Price needs to average above $40k.
- Utilization is the risk. About 15-30 sprints/year cannot keep 3-4 full-time scientists busy, so use a contractor network (the Alacrita model). Retainers smooth revenue.
- LLM translation and extraction cuts hours but is not a moat; Perceptic and Patsnap are funded to commoditize it.
- Cheaper data: license Redica and Kharon-type feeds rather than build them. FDA also promised to publish more foreign-site inspection information, so building a database is the wrong investment.

## 6. Regulatory and liability landscape

- **FDA acceptance.** [Goodwin](https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/09/insights-lifesciences-fda-sharpens-oversight-tools-on-global-clinical-trial-data) (Sep 2026): FDA plans more BIMO inspections including foreign Phase 1, updated country-risk site selection, and public flagging of sites that deny access. Sponsors should treat access as "a material factor." FDA retains authority under 21 CFR 312.120 to refuse nonconforming data; no specific 2026 rejection was identified.
- **Congress.** Reps. Moolenaar and Cline asked FDA to reject China-generated data unless the site was FDA-audited within 12 months, after three trial deaths in China ([PharmaVoice](https://www.pharmavoice.com/news/china-clinical-trial-deaths-fda-oversight/829502/); letter date is Aug 20 or 21 depending on source). A House Appropriations report would bar FDA from considering China-site data in INDs, but it is report language, not law, and "highly uncertain" ([Hogan Lovells](https://www.hlc.com/en/publications/house-committee-report-signals-limits-on-foreign-clinical-data)). It advises factoring these restrictions into valuation. This is the strongest demand driver.
- **BIOSECURE.** OMB's first list is due Dec 18, 2026, but the effect is phased: guidance within 180 days, FAR changes within a year, prohibitions 60-90 days later, potentially nearly three years out. A court preliminarily enjoined WuXi AppTec's 1260H designation on Aug 7, 2026, though OMB can still list it via a separate pathway ([Greenberg Traurig](https://www.gtlaw.com/en/insights/2026/9/biosecure-act-update-court-enjoins-wuxi-apptecs-1260h-designation-but-strategic-and-compliance-clocks-keep-running)). It governs federal contracts and grants, so it touches licensing indirectly via CRO/CDMO dependence.
- **China data rules.** Provision of HGR information to foreign parties needs NHC filing; outbound personal data needs CAC steps that can take months, and the source advises against assuming data flows at signing ([Morgan Lewis](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/05/strategic-compliance-navigating-hgr-and-data-risks-in-china-life-sciences-transactions)). The May 2026 NHC draft would narrow "HGR information" to nucleic-acid sequence data, which may ease clinical raw-data sharing, but I could not confirm it is final [G]. GT also flags PRC State Council Order 837 (effective Jul 1, 2026) as a possible constraint on know-how transfer; its reach is unverified [G].
- **Privilege.** The "report sits under privilege" pitch is weaker than it sounds. Kovel-type protection requires counsel to retain the consultant and the work to support legal advice, not business decisions ([ABA overview](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/litigation/resources/newsletters/professional-liability/privilege-work-product-kovel-update-recent-case-law/), general doctrine). Commercial diligence is exposed.
- **Liability.** A verification miss on a deal worth hundreds of millions invites claims. Needs counsel-engaged structure, scope-limited opinions, liability caps and E&O cover. I found no E&O pricing or case law for scientific diligence providers [G].

## 7. Is the why-now real?

- **Deal flow: real.** Record H1 2026 and rising upfronts.
- **FDA/Congress scrutiny: real and new.** August-September 2026 actions raise the cost of unverifiable China data, and the Phase 1 inspection expansion hits exactly the early packages this service targets.
- **BIOSECURE: overstated.** The Dec 18 list is a date, not a spend trigger. Supply-chain mapping would be a 2027+ revenue line in a crowded space.
- **Layoffs: mixed.** BioSpace counted 14,167 biopharma job cuts Jan 1-May 15, 2026, up 24% YoY (via a [Cassel Salpeter clip](https://www.casselsalpeter.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CS-Media-Clip-Biospace-05.20.26.docx.pdf)), but [Fierce](https://www.fiercebiotech.com/biotech/biopharma-recruiters-seeing-signs-recovery-layoffs-stay-cool-q326) says announcements cooled in Q2-Q3 2026. The needed profile (bilingual, GLP/CMC regulatory depth) is a tiny subset; no supply data exists [G].

## 8. Moat and synthesis

| Moat | Rating | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Network effects | Weak | None |
| Switching costs | Weak to moderate | Retainer relationships only |
| Scale economies | Weak | Labor-intensive |
| Intangibles (trust, track record, named scientists) | Moderate, only if earned | The only defensible asset |

Durable edge: a track record of red flags that later proved right, plus law-firm referral relationships. Structural vulnerabilities: seller data access, commodity data inputs, AI-assisted incumbents, liability exposure, and a revenue ceiling that caps hiring.

## 9. Corrections to the prior research file

- Vision Lifesciences was missing from the competitor list and weakens the "nobody sells this" claim.
- The "BIOSECURE lists in about three months" framing is accurate on date but misleading on effect.
- Redica's NMPA coverage was unverified before; I found no evidence of it as of Jan 2026.
- Hogan Lovells' note that the House restriction is non-binding was not previously captured.

## 10. Highest-value next tests

1. Price check: ask 5 NewCo VCs and 5 mid-cap BD heads what they paid for China diligence in the last 12 months and what they would pay.
2. Pilot through law-firm introductions at $20k, scoped as a term-sheet-stage red-flag memo plus a re-check before signing, not a 72-hour promise.
3. Test a seller-side "diligence-ready package" review with 3 Chinese licensors.
4. Get a quote for E&O cover before the first sale.

# I1172-M2 Dossier: Home Equity Assurance for Data Center Neighbors

Researched 13 Oct 2026 (about 40 searches and fetches). Tags: [C] cited fact, [I] my inference, [U] unverified or search-summary only.

## 1. Bottom line

The problem is real and developers are already paying for it, but in other forms. The structure as written has three serious weaknesses.

- **Insurance classification.** The one regulator ruling I found treats a pay-on-sale home-value guarantee as prohibited financial guaranty insurance.
- **Payout economics.** Sale-price noise alone is probably enough to drain the proposed escrow.
- **Buyouts.** Developers' actual 2026 answer is buyouts, not guarantees.

The bottom-up market is tens of millions of dollars a year at best, not hundreds of millions. I found no buyer, RFP or paid pilot for a third-party guarantee. The idea is **conditionally alive, in a narrower form** (section 9).

## 2. Direct competitors: none found; real substitutes are numerous

**No productized, third-party data-center home-value guarantee found.** Searches for developer, startup or insurer offerings returned nothing; insurer results covered only facility-side cover ([Reed Smith](https://www.reedsmith.com/articles/insurance-coverage-data-centers-navigating-challenges-adapting-marketplace/)). "Not found" is not proof of absence. Crunchbase and PitchBook were not checked, and I could not find any record of Prevolt's funding [U].

**Developer-run substitutes (the budget this idea would redirect):**

- **Buyouts.** Nscale's "Good Neighbors" program in Mason County, WV offers the highest of three valuations plus a "material premium" and pays closing costs ([WCHS](https://wchstv.com/news/local/voluntary-buyout-offers-rolled-out-for-meadowlands-estates-homes-near-data-center)). About 15 of 53 homes had sold or were in process by June 2026 ([WSAZ](https://www.wsaz.com/2026/06/10/mason-county-data-center-developer-nscale-offering-buy-neighboring-homes/)). The homes become employee and contractor housing. [C]
- **Howell Township, MI.** The developer's attorney offered sale at appraised value plus 1% within 1,000 ft, plus an unspecified 2,500 ft tier ([WXYZ](https://www.wxyz.com/news/howell-township-data-center-informational-meeting-held)). [U]
- **DeForest, WI.** A draft QTS agreement would have bought homes within 1/4 mile at no less than 110% of assessed value if "materially adversely affected". The deal collapsed in January 2026, before any annexation vote ([Wisconsin Watch](https://wisconsinwatch.org/2026/08/wisconsin-deforest-data-center-deal-guaranteed-tax-revenue-river-improvements-affordable-housing/)). [C]
- **Lump sums.** NorthPoint (Hazle Township, PA) offered $10k to each of about 4,500 households ($45M, inside a $165M community benefits package) and was met with "are they trying to bribe us" ([Bisnow](https://www.bisnow.com/news/philadelphia/data-center-community-relations/northpoint-hazle-resident-checks-pennsylvania), [Propmodo](https://propmodo.com/cash-to-residents-is-the-newest-tool-in-the-data-center-fight/)). The offer is dated June 2026. Press accounts disagree on whether the township rejected the project before or after it. [C]

**Legislative substitute.** Illinois HB4319 (introduced 2026) would pay owners within 1,000 ft 1.5x their proven fair-market-value decline. It uses a certified appraisal at developer cost and allows suit after 90 days. A county-association group lists it as "Oppose", and I found no evidence it has passed ([ISAC](https://www.isacoil.org/ea309cec-8887-4476-b965-60d75b5f1b75/bill-details/)). [C] If something like it passes, a private guarantee could become a negotiated alternative or a safe harbor. [I]

**Historical analogs of the product itself (all weak track record):**

- **Municipal programs.** Oak Park, IL (1970s) reportedly never paid a claim ([Wikipedia summary of Shiller and Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_equity_protection)). Chicago's tax-funded districts saw few cash claims, though one district held about $9.6M ([WWNO](https://www.wwno.org/2014-06-24/chicago-program-designed-to-prevent-white-flight-gets-renewed-attention)).
- **Syracuse pilot (2002).** One-time fee of 1.5% of home value.
- **Home Value Insurance Co.** It sold only 172 policies, went into Ohio rehabilitation in 2012, and was dissolved in January 2013 ([Insurance Journal](https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2012/09/18/263329.htm)). [U]
- **Working Equity / Home Value Protection.** CB Insights lists it as dead ([CB Insights](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/home-value-protection)).
- **Home Diversification Corp.** A junior-lien contract at about $19/month, launched in 2019 ([MPA](https://www.mpamag.com/us/mortgage-industry/market-updates/fintech-startup-to-launch-home-equity-protection-product/179747)).

All of these were consumer-paid or taxpayer-funded and index-based. None was a developer-funded, locally negotiated escrow, so this idea is structurally new. [I]

**Sensor vendors** (KETOS, Aethair, Envirosuite, Kunak) from the parent research share no product, buyer budget or moat with this mutation. Not re-verified.

## 3. Incumbents who could add this

- **Fund administrators (Epiq, Kroll, JND).** Epiq already acts as administrator and escrow or QSF manager, usually paired with a bank as escrow agent ([Epiq](https://epiqglobal.com/en-us/services/class-action-mass-tort/mass-torts/mass-tort-fund-administration-payments)). A vendor blog puts QSF administration at 0.25 to 1.5% of assets a year, $2.5k to $15k setup, and $150 to $500 per disbursement ([LegalSoft](https://www.legalsoft.com/blog/settlement-fund-management)). That source is weak. [C]
  - They have the neutrality, bank relationships and track record a county attorney wants, and face no counterparty-credit objection to a 10-year obligation. [I]
  - They lack valuation models, the one real differentiator here.
- **Title and escrow firms, AVM vendors and appraisal management companies.** They hold the data and closing-table access but do not sell neutrality or a county-approved formula. [I]
- **Law firms and consultancies.** They already draft community benefit agreements. The Columbia Law piece describes property value guarantees as an existing CBA clause, with the developer guaranteeing appraised value as of a date, usually ending on sale ([Columbia](https://blogs.law.columbia.edu/climatechange/2026/05/28/community-benefits-agreements-and-data-center-development/)). It does not say who administers them. [C]

The moat is thin. The mechanics are copyable; the defensible assets are the price-effect model, county relationships and first track record. [I]

## 4. Bottom-up market size

**Where the exposure is growing:**

- Large (50+ MW) data centers rose from 49 in 2018 to 347 in 2026.
- ZIP codes hosting one rose from 12 (2015) to 108 (June 2026), with 125 projected by year-end.
- About 1.5% of US home sales fall within 5 miles of a large facility, projected at 2.3% once the 2027 pipeline lands.
- The median 2026 facility sits in an area with about 70% fewer residential units per square mile than 2017 openings, about 27 miles from the city center.

Source for all four: Realtor.com's August 2026 report as summarized by [HousingWire](https://www.housingwire.com/articles/data-center-boom-is-putting-more-homes-near-facilities/). The Realtor.com page itself was blocked to me. [C]

**Reachable buyers.**

- Data Center Watch counted at least 75 projects (about $130B) disrupted by local opposition in Q1 2026 ([DCW](https://datacenterwatch.org/q1-2026)). Another outlet attributes 45 projects (about $68B) to Q2 ([AI Weekly](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/data-center-watch-45-us-ai-data-center-projects-worth-68b-blocked-or-delayed-in)). DCW does not define "disrupted" publicly. [C]
- Annualizing gives about 240 contested projects a year. These are the buyers with acute need. [I]

**Households per project.**

- Observed range: 53 homes (Mason), about 150 (Ashburn Regency), about 4,500 (Hazle).
- Falling density means typical new sites have fewer neighbors. I assume 300 to 1,500 enrollable households. [I]

**Revenue per program, at the idea's own price points:**

| Program size | Enrollment at $300 | 1%/yr escrow fee | Claim fees | Year 1 total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 households | $300k | $40k | ~$45-75k/yr | ~$0.4M |
| 3,000 households | $900k | $120k | ~$135-225k/yr | ~$1.0-1.2M |

Claim fees assume every sale is adjudicated. The idea's "$1M+ per program" requires a top-end site of about 3,000 households. [I]

**Ceiling and realistic capture.** If all 240 contested projects bought at 1,000 households each, the ceiling is about $70 to 100M a year. Realistic early capture of 5 to 10% is about $4 to 10M a year: a services business, not software. [I]

**Float.** The 3-month Treasury yield is 4.26% as of 13 Oct 2026 ([Treasury](https://home.treasury.gov/resource-center/data-chart-center/interest-rates/TextView?type=daily_treasury_yield_curve&field_tdr_date_value_month=202610)). That gives about $0.5M a year on a $12M escrow. A custodian bank will keep most of it. [C/I]

## 5. Evidence of demand and willingness to pay

**Residents want value protection, not checks.**

- A Hazle retiree said $10k "doesn't match how much it's going to tank my property value" ([Reason](https://reason.com/2026/09/28/data-centers-and-their-discontents/)).
- Property values were also raised at Yorkville IL, East Whiteland PA and Decatur Township IN hearings in 2026 (search summaries) [U].
- Propmodo expects future offers tied to "utility bill credits or property value guarantees". That is a prediction, not an observation. [C]

**Developers can afford it.**

- Shell-and-core cost is about $11.3M per MW (JLL via [Datacentres.com](https://www.datacentres.com/news/data-centre-construction-costs-11m-per-mw)). A 300 MW campus like Hazle is therefore about $3.4B, so a $4M escrow is roughly 0.1% of shell-and-core. Willingness to be the obligor is the issue, not budget. [C/I]

**What is missing.**

- No developer I found has offered a value guarantee.
- Sabey, in Indianapolis, answered value objections with an appraiser opinion, the George Mason study and a commissioned Integra study (80 homes within 1.5 mi appreciated 42% against 41% locally). The commission approved variances on 18 March 2026 ([Mirror Indy](https://mirrorindy.org/sabey-data-centers-indianapolis-property-values-protect-decatur-township/), [Bisnow](https://www.bisnow.com/news/national/data-center-community-relations/data-centers-may-not-be-a-drag-on-nearby-home-prices-135084)). [C]
- I found no RFP, county ordinance or paid pilot for a neutral administrator.

**Wind precedent is thin.**

- A Maine bill, an Iowa county ordinance draft and Illinois agreements exist.
- One Illinois county plan reportedly lapsed unused, and developers call such guarantees "unworkable" (search summaries of [Maine LD 1042](https://legislature.maine.gov/legis/bills/bills_125th/billtexts/HP077601.asp), [SD PUC docket](https://puc.sd.gov/commission/dockets/electric/2018/EL18-053/prefiledexhibits/intervenors/jonhenslin/jw4.pdf)). [U]
- The idea's claim that counties and lawyers "recognize the form" is only partly supported.

**Pitch angle.** The average effect on home values looks near zero in several studies:

- Realtor.com: 43 matched ZIPs, no meaningful change two years after activation.
- George Mason University: homes closer to data centers sold for more, with caveats.
- NAR: a 25% positive versus 22% negative agent split. NAR notes county data "can't tell us what happens to an individual home next to a facility" ([NAR](https://www.nar.realtor/newsroom/theres-no-single-data-center-effect-on-housing-markets-nar-report-finds), [GMU](https://schar.gmu.edu/news/2025-11/study-home-prices-are-higher-when-house-near-data-center)). [C]

If a developer believes those studies, a guarantee is a cheap, credible signal. [I]

Two counterpoints. A Princeton thesis attributes its pooled null to small sites with no effect mixed with larger sites with negative effects ([Princeton](https://theses-dissertations.princeton.edu/entities/publication/f5612f3e-e79f-45b3-93f3-5f38e4c97f11)), and guarantees will be demanded at the largest projects. [U/I] Realtor.com also found data-center ZIPs kept 66% of pre-opening active listings after three years, against 43% in matched ZIPs, which suggests slower absorption and matters for a "listed 60+ days" rule. [C/I]

## 6. Unit economics

**Valuation costs.** Older, undated sources put AVMs at about $20+, BPOs at $50 to $150 and appraisals at $300 to $500 ([NMP](https://nationalmortgageprofessional.com/news/61564/appraisals-avms-bpos-which-should-mortgage-professionals-choose), [NMP REO](https://nationalmortgageprofessional.com/news/23685/reo-avm-compared-other-valuation-methods)). The idea's $300 BPO looks high. AVM plus BPO is plausibly $70 to $170, so enrollment gross margin could be 40 to 75% before outreach, portal and call-center costs. Those costs are not in the idea. [C/I]

**Payout risk, the main finding.** The product is a put option on one house's sale price, so noise creates payouts even when the true data-center effect is zero. [I]

- Individual house prices have annual standard deviations of roughly 12 to 15% against city indexes (Case and Shiller 1989 reports about 15% for individual houses, and a later paper about 12%, per search results; I did not open the papers). [U]
- Assume a terminal sale-versus-reference dispersion of 8 to 12%, which includes AVM and BPO error in the frozen reference. I assume a $300k home and a 40% chance of sale in 10 years. NAR's median seller tenure is 11 years ([NAR](https://www.nar.realtor/magazine/real-estate-news/nar-2025-profile-of-home-buyers-sellers-reveals-market-extremes)). [C/I]
- Result: expected payout per sale is about 3 to 4.5% of value ($9.6k to $13.6k) with a 20% cap. That is about $3.8k to $5.4k per enrolled household, against a $3 to 5k escrow.
- The idea's assumption that 10 to 30% of escrow is paid out is therefore likely too low several-fold.
- A 10% deductible (pay only the shortfall beyond 10%) cuts expected payout to about $0.5k to $1.4k per household, roughly 10 to 45% of a $3 to 5k escrow. That is workable.
- A simulation study priced at-the-money index puts at 0.6% to 20.85% of index value between pre- and post-crisis periods ([JABR](https://clutejournals.com/index.php/JABR/article/view/8884)). The control-index adjustment removes most of that market-wide risk. The remaining risk is basis risk: rural exurbs have few comparable sales, so the control index will be noisy. [I]

**Adverse selection.** Opt-in enrollment attracts owners who expect to sell low. The arm's-length rule and the cap help but do not fix it. [I]

## 7. Regulation and liability

**Insurance law is the gating risk.** New York's insurance department counsel ruled that a plan paying homeowners on sale if a ZIP index fell is insurance under §1101(a) and financial guaranty insurance under §6901(a)(1)(D), which is not permitted ([NY DFS OGC 08-07-31](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/insurance/ogco2008/rg080731.htm)). It also distinguished an earlier index-only program. It named no permissible structure. [C]

- A UConn law-review abstract says states differ on classification and warns that index-linking does not by itself avoid insurance treatment ([UConn](https://insurancelawreview.rso.uconn.edu/?p=1638)). [C]
- The idea says "a contract, not insurance" with a developer as obligor. That is untested. The better argument is that a developer settling its own neighbor-relations exposure is not "doing an insurance business" and the administrator is not the obligor. [I]
- I found no state-by-state analysis. A counsel opinion is the right first spend.

**Other issues.**

- Counties that sign must avoid terms that invite regulatory takings claims (Columbia, above). [C]
- Pennsylvania's governor has banned NDAs between local governments and data center companies. Any deal will be public ([Propmodo](https://propmodo.com/cash-to-residents-is-the-newest-tool-in-the-data-center-fight/)). [C]
- Developer counsel may treat a pre-committed payout as an admission; I found no direct evidence either way. [I]
- Some states restrict BPO use, so valuations may need licensed appraisers in those states. [U]

## 8. Is the why-now real?

**Verified:**

- NY Executive Order 62: 14 July 2026, 50 MW and up. It pauses only certain discretionary DEC approvals and explicitly excludes local permits ([DWT](https://www.dwt.com/blogs/energy--environmental-law-blog/2026/07/ny-data-center-permitting-pause-executive-order-62)).
- Texas: 21 Sept 2026 order to TCEQ to pause data-center permits until the ERCOT and water audits finish, expected mid-December ([Bracewell](https://www.bracewell.com/resources/governor-abbott-orders-tceq-to-pause-all-permit-issuance-for-data-center-projects/)).
- Realtor.com's 108 ZIPs (section 4).

**Qualification.** The NY and Texas pauses are grid and water actions. They pause approvals and do not by themselves create demand for neighbor guarantees. [I]

**Stronger why-now evidence.**

- Opposition is scaling: more than 300 state bills in six weeks, and opposition groups going from 396 to 833 in one quarter (DCW, above; the group counts come from a secondary summary [U]).
- A bill like HB4319 is a credible threat.
- NAR released a county-level report on 8 to 9 Sept 2026 that explicitly cannot speak to individual homes. That leaves the individual-home question open. [C]

**Not verified:** the "4-bedroom listed 15 to 18% lower" anecdote, and a Loudoun "2.8% lower within 0.5 mile" finding. A direct search did not corroborate the second. Do not use either in outreach. [U]

## 9. Strongest version and what would kill it

**Narrow the wedge.**

- Sell developers a **buyout alternative or complement**: a guarantee for owners who stay, run by a neutral administrator.
- Use a **10% deductible**, a smaller cap and an index-based trigger where possible.
- Build it as a **county-approved development-agreement rider** (DeForest-style, but with a neutral administrator).
- Partner with an established bank or administrator (Epiq-class) as obligor-of-record or successor, to answer counterparty-credit concerns.

**Timing realism.** DeForest staff met QTS for about seven months before announcement, and the deal died three weeks later. A 90-day gate to a signed pilot is optimistic. [C/I]

**Kill triggers.**

1. Counsel in two or three target states says the structure is insurance.
2. No developer will be obligor of record after 10 outreach calls.
3. Developers prefer buyouts and treat guarantees as a worse version.
4. No county adopts a rider within about 6 months.

## 10. Gaps

- No evidence of anyone paying a neutral party for this.
- Wind-guarantee claim and payout data not found.
- HVIC's failure cause beyond a capital shortfall is not documented here.
- Realtor.com's primary report was blocked; households-per-project is assumed.
- Prevolt and Jambo funding not found.
- Illinois HB4319 sponsor and status unconfirmed (ilga.gov failed certificate verification).

# I1175 Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion. Validation Dossier (2026-10-13)

## Verdict
The pain and the lender-paid demand are real, but the "GAP" label from the earlier check does not hold. GreenLancer already sells lender-paid completion plus permit/interconnection remediation. Lenders and servicers are building in-house capacity. The completion market is small and lumpy (my estimate: roughly $3-10M a year serviceable, see section 5). Anyone who takes a permit over must hold a contractor license and accepts liability for the dead installer's work. Recommendation: WOUNDED, not dead. Only the sharper angle (portfolio triage for servicers and credit unions, then success-fee cure) is worth testing, and only after 6-8 buyer calls.

## 1. Is the why-now real? Yes, with a timing catch
- Freedom Forever filed Chapter 11 on Apr 15, 2026 and converted to Chapter 7 on Aug 7. Claims are due Oct 16, 2026. About 1,600 workers were reportedly laid off. The court let Credit Human, EnFin, EverBright, GoodLeap, Participate, Project Solar and Sunrun take over unfinished projects, hire contractors and push systems to PTO without separate motions. GoodLeap got explicit authority to take physical possession of hardware. [pv magazine](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/09/09/Freedom-Forever-Bankruptcy-Converted-To-Chapter-7-Liquidation-Key-Dates-Set/)
- Freedom Forever was reportedly the second-largest installer in 2025, with a 6.1% share per Wood Mackenzie. Sources disagree on its rank. [pv magazine](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/04/15/residential-solar-company-freedom-forever-files-chapter-11-bankruptcy/)
- Causes: the 25D credit expired at the end of 2025, Wood Mackenzie sees about a 20% volume drop in 2026, and Mosaic (its largest creditor, over $110M) filed in June 2025. [Latitude Media](https://www.latitudemedia.com/news/what-freedom-forevers-bankruptcy-says-about-residential-solar-today/)
- Q2 2026 residential installs were 995 MW, down 12% year over year and the lowest quarter in five years. Wood Mackenzie now forecasts a 23% full-year decline. [Mercom](https://mercomindia.com/us-solar-installations-jump-45-yoy-to-11-4-gw-in-q2-2026) Customer acquisition cost is forecast up 40% to $0.84/W. [Wood Mackenzie](https://woodmac.com/news/opinion/us-residential-solar-customer-acquisition-costs-set-to-spike-40-in-2026-before-gradual-decline/)
- Solar Insure counts 100+ installer closures since 2023. [Solar Insure](https://www.solarinsure.com/solar-bankruptcies-hub) Solar-loan ABS net losses were 3.67% annualized in July 2026, up 84 bps year over year. [KBRA](https://www.kbra.com/publications/ccYPfsKf/u.s.-solar-loan-abs-index-july-2026)
- Catch: the biggest failure's first wave is already staffed. A financier deal was approved Apr 24 [Law360](https://www.law360.co.uk/articles/2469813), and the stay-relief order is roughly two months old. Most Freedom Forever systems were third-party-owned leases and PPAs, so the financiers own those assets and have the most reason to finish them in-house. [Solar Power World](https://www.solarpowerworldonline.com/2026/06/what-homeowners-should-do-after-freedom-forever-filed-for-bankruptcy/)

Strong signals:

It reports 200+ field partners and uses SolarGrade software for documentation. This is promotional and unaudited. [PR Newswire](https://www.streetinsider.com/PRNewswire/GreenLancer+and+SolarGrade+Partner+to+Deliver+Premier+Solar+Field+Services/26097204.html), [Solar Builder](https://solarbuildermag.com/operations-maintenance/greenlancer-finds-solar-orphan-om-partner-in-solargrade/)

- Solar Servicing (Forbright Bank) hired a "pipeline team" for partially funded Mosaic loans. [Solar Power World](https://www.solarpowerworldonline.com/2025/09/solar-servicing-acquires-mosaic-assets-resumes-pv-lending/)
- A lender told a consumer attorney in a deposition that 40% of its installers had gone out of business. GoodLeap says it now has a team for customers whose contractor is gone, and one Texas borrower is still billed on a $67,000 loan. [CBS Texas](https://www.cbsnews.com/texas/news/bankruptcies-leave-some-solar-customers-with-broken-panels/)

Tucson Old Pueblo Credit Union fully funded 39 member loans of $30-35k on more than $1M of unbuilt or unfinished work, paused payments, and ended up-front full funding. [KVOA](https://www.kvoa.com/news/n4t-investigators-dozens-left-paying-for-unfinished-solar-jobs-that-lender-fully-funded/article_7bfef5c6-137b-11ed-a968-a785ad6288a3.html), [DOJ](https://www.justice.gov/usao-az/pr/solar-company-owner-indicted-fraud)

## 4. Pressure on the "non-obvious insight"
- GreenLancer's own release says permit and warranty documentation is "often unavailable or erroneous." The records-recovery thesis is already its stated pain point.
- Records are not purely locked. Tucson Electric Power's orphan process lets the new installer submit the customer's records release, keeps the original interconnection clock, and refuses reassignment by the dead installer. The customer, not the lender, has the authority. [TEP](https://docs.tep.com/wp-content/uploads/Orphan-FAQs-for-Installers.pdf) This is one utility, so I cannot generalize.
- "Lenders can't see which loans are dark" is weak for loans funded in milestones. M2 is paid at installation and M3 (often about 10%) at utility approval, so the originator can see which jobs lack PTO. [EnergySage](https://www.energysage.com/news/mosaic-files-for-bankruptcy/) Visibility is probably worse on acquired legacy books and bank or credit-union holdings. That is untested.
- ABS trustees are a weak second wave. In Mosaic Solar 2021-2, pre-PTO loans were capped at 10% of the pool with a repurchase obligation. [ABS Report](https://asreport.americanbanker.com/news/mosaic-solar-trust-issues-191-million-in-abs) Stranded pre-PTO loans mostly sit with originators, warehouse lenders, banks and credit unions. - Assume 25-50% reaches independent vendors, since the seven financiers keep much in-house or with GreenLancer. At $2.5-3k all-in, that is roughly $1-7M, one time.
- Ongoing: 100+ closures since 2023 at 20-50 unfinished jobs each (Tucson Solar Pros had 39 loans, Empire 45 homes) gives roughly 600-1,400 jobs a year, or $2-4M a year at about $3k.
- Dashboard: 10-25 realistic buyers at an assumed $25-60k a year is $0.25-1.5M a year, with no pricing evidence.
- Total: about $3-10M a year in a good year. That is a services business, not venture-scale.
- Do not use the "820,000", "500,000+" or Titan "150,000 households" figures. I could not verify them. Titan said it had helped over 100,000 households, which is not a stranded count. - Closest analog is mortgage property preservation, where lender-paid field work is priced to caps. Fannie Mae's June 2025 allowables raised initial securing from $250 to $325 (secondary source). [summary](https://lakemeadmobilenotary.com/insights/fnma-svc-2025-03-property-preservation-expense-limit-increases-nevada) Vendors report about $19.85 per work order in administrative and tech cost before service costs. ## 7. Regulatory and liability landscape
- Licensing is the hardest barrier. In California an unlicensed contractor cannot sue to collect compensation for work needing a license. [B&P 7031](https://california.public.law/codes/business_and_professions_code_section_7031) The C-46 solar class needs about four years of journey-level experience and a $25k bond per a secondary source. [CSLB](https://www.cslb.ca.gov/About_Us/Library/Licensing_Classifications/Licensing_Classifications_Detail.aspx?Class=C46), [guide](https://contractorlicenserequirements.com/california/solar-license-requirements/) Other states vary: Arizona CR-17 and Nevada C-2g per the same guide. Subcontracting labor does not remove the need for a licensed contractor of record. Oregon tightened solar licensing on June 5, 2026. [Energy Trust](https://blog.energytrust.org/?p=13916)
- Taking over a permit carries liability. Florida's Sunrise form has the new contractor accept responsibility for correcting prior work. [Sunrise](https://sunrisefl.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/8456/638464612289300000) Dana Point may cancel and reissue the permit, require a "special investigation" of unpermitted work, and charge fees. [Dana Point](https://danapoint.org/home/showpublisheddocument/30946/637267090685100000) New Castle County requires owner consent and a termination notice. [New Castle](https://www.newcastlede.gov/DocumentCenter/View/476/Change-of-Contractor-Requirements-PDF)
- Lender exposure creates demand. The FTC Holder Rule lets borrowers assert installer claims against loan holders, generally capped at amounts paid. The CFPB flagged hidden dealer fees in 2024, and dealer-fee TILA suits are surviving motions to dismiss. [Ballard Spahr](https://www.consumerfinancemonitor.com/2026/03/26/todays-podcast-episode-residential-solar-finance-under-intensifying-scrutiny-key-regulatory-and-litigation-trends/) Connecticut has about 65 complaints against SunStrong [CT AG](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/attorney-general-tong-announces-new-developments-to-hold-solar-industry-accountable), and Texas AG demands went to Freedom Forever and Sunrun. [Solar Power World](https://www.solarpowerworldonline.com/2026/04/texas-attorney-general-launches-investigation-into-residential-solar-sales-practices/)
- State recovery funds are weak: Minnesota's requires a civil judgment and a licensed contractor, so the lender is the realistic payer.
- Not researched: insurance cost for completion work, data-privacy limits on cross-matching loan tapes against utility records, and utility-by-utility interconnection rules beyond TEP.

# I0836-M2 Dossier: Lender-Required Curtailment Runway Reports for Data Centers

Prepared 2026-10-13. Evidence grades: [P] primary document read this session; [S] trade, law-firm or secondary page read; [V] vendor claim; [U] page blocked, relying on a search-engine summary only.

## Verdict

Conditional. The problem is real, the regulatory drivers are real, and I found no company selling this to lenders. But four things in the pitch do not hold up as written. (1) The "roughly 100 hours" premise is wrong as stated; the binding number is the state permit and it varies. (2) I found no evidence that any lender, rating agency or regulation requires or budgets for this report. (3) The bottom-up market is probably $1.5-6M a year, not $10M. (4) PJM's curtailment regime is not final. Proceed only to the 30-day demand test, with the kill criteria in section 8.

## 1. The legal premise is narrower than the pitch

- Federal text [P]: emergency engines have "no time limit" in emergency situations, 100 hours a year for maintenance and readiness testing, and up to 50 of those hours for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, except under a financial arrangement when a local balancing authority or distribution operator dispatches to avert local voltage collapse or overloads. [40 CFR 63.6640(f)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/63.6640). The pitch's "100 hours" is the testing and non-emergency cap, not a cap on running during a true outage.
- EPA's May 2025 interpretation (Duke Energy's mandatory program) loosened one corner of the 50-hour rule and said EPA is "evaluating more substantive changes" ([EPA](https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-issues-clarification-help-power-data-centers-ensure-us-ai-capital-world) [P]; [Kirkland](https://www.kirkland.com/publications/kirkland-alert/2025/05/new-epa-guidance-clarifies-when-data-centers-and-other-operators-may-utilize-emergency-backup) [S]). A compliance vendor says facilities inside an ISO/RTO cannot use the 50 hours for demand response and that most data center generator capacity cannot participate ([Facilities Dive](https://www.facilitiesdive.com/news/why-demand-response-participation-remains-fraught-with-risk-1/822506/) [V]). I could not independently verify that vendor, which is called BackupPower AI.
- The real constraint is the site's synthetic-minor permit. Virginia caps total engine hours at 500 a year including emergencies, and treats any use of the 50 federal non-emergency hours as non-emergency operation with stricter state controls ([Trinity](http://trinityconsultants.com/news/virginia-department-of-environmental-quality-releases-three-air-permitting-guidance-documents-for-data-centers) [S]). Virginia has permitted more than 9,000 diesel emergency generators at data centers, and the article's example of a 3,000-hour pooled limit for 50 engines notes it could be used up in one extended outage ([Williams Mullen](https://www.williamsmullen.com/insights/news/legal-news/frequently-asked-air-questions-faaqs-understanding-data-center-emergency) [S]). This supports the product: runway is permit-specific and nobody publishes it. It also means a lender's counsel will reject a headline "100 hours".
- Texas SB 6 [P]: 75 MW+ loads must disclose on-site backup generation (defined as non-exporting and able to serve at least 50% of on-site demand). ERCOT may direct them to deploy it or curtail, and the subsection does not authorize "a violation of any emissions limitation" ([bill text](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)).
- Counter-force. DOE used Federal Power Act 202(c) on May 18-20, 2026 to let PJM deploy data center backup generation as a last resort ([DOE](https://www.energy.gov/ceser/federal-power-act-section-202c-pjm-interconnection-llc-pjm-order-no-202-26-23) [P]). Gibson Dunn reports it required compliance with ancillary environmental requirements "to the maximum extent feasible", not a blanket waiver ([Gibson Dunn](https://www.gibsondunn.com/doe-emergency-order-signals-new-role-for-data-centers-backup-power/) [S]). A search summary says a different 202(c) order (OUC) did override permit limits [U]. In a federally declared emergency the permit cap may be set aside, which shrinks the loss scenario.
- Open question that is also the product: PJM's new curtailment tool (IRAS) fires at a potential Energy Emergency Alert level 1 with 10 minutes to comply [P, [PJM deck](https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/large-load/iras-training.pdf)]. EPA's emergency examples are interruptions of utility power. A directed shift to generators at EEA1 looks closer to non-emergency demand response. I found no EPA or state guidance on this. The report would therefore carry an attorney's interpretation, which is both the value and the liability.

## 2. Why now: real but unsettled

- PJM's 2028/29 auction cleared at the cap and was 6,831 MW short ([PJM release](https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/newsroom/2026-releases/20260714-pjm-capacity-auction-procures-138318-mw-of-generation-resources.pdf), from the parent file; not re-opened).
- IRAS was filed Aug 13, 2026 for a June 1, 2027 start; PJM's Sept 25 training deck still says "Pending FERC approval" [P]. On Sept 29 FERC accepted but suspended the companion backstop procurement to Feb 28, 2027 ([Public Power](https://www.publicpower.org/node/31356) [S]). I found no IRAS ruling.
- IRAS only reaches New Large Loads (50 MW+, in service after June 1, 2027) without their own new capacity. Total curtailment is capped at the lesser of the new load or the shortage, and ends if unneeded for three straight delivery years [P, same deck]. The PJM Board expects curtailment "infrequently, for limited durations", and says large loads may "move to their backup generators" ([June 1 letter](https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2026/20260602-board-response-to-njpbu-connect-and-manage-scope.pdf) [P]). Already-financed campuses are untouched.
- Useful for the pitch: PJM's Large Load Registry will collect "Backup generation (MW), including fuel type and relevant permitting limitations" [P, same deck]. PJM treats permit limits as material. But registry access is limited to commissions, utilities, the market monitor and FERC; the public sees aggregates only. Borrowers will assemble the file; no one gets a public dataset moat.
- ERCOT: an Aurora study for Google and V-Wire (Sept 2026) finds fully grid-exposed controllable loads curtailed 50-241 hours a year on average across three sites (2028-30, central weather year), and 35-550 hours across weather years ([Aurora/ERCOT](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/09/10/Curtailment-Mitigation-for-PCLRs-Modeling-the-Effects-of-Front-of-Meter-Netting_LLWG.pdf) [P]). That is the strongest evidence that exposure can exceed per-engine caps. The PUCT's September 2026 large-load rule, as reported, covers fees and energization milestones and not backup generation ([Utility Dive](https://utilitydive.com/news/texas-puc-adopts-data-center-interconnection-rules/830899) [S]); ERCOT's tracker shows the backup-generation trigger unfinished ([ERCOT](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2025/09/15/89th-Legislative-Session-PPTX-ERCOT-Status-September-2026.pdf) [S]).

Net: credible for new-build PJM and ERCOT campuses, but it becomes a credit term only after IRAS and ERCOT's trigger are final. Expect 2027 at earliest.

## 3. Demand and willingness to pay

Supported:
- Lenders do "significant" power diligence ([Davis Polk on 9fin](https://www.davispolk.com/news/elena-millerman-discusses-due-diligence-data-center-financings-9fin) [S]); S&P frames execution, cost and resilience power risks as credit risks ([S&P](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/research/2026/07/more-power-less-cushion-ai-and-the-changing-credit-risk-profile-of-data-centers) [U]); a land broker says lenders should treat curtailment as a diligence line ([Landgate](https://www.landgate.com/news/pjm-just-made-grid-power-conditional-for-data-centers) [S], low authority).
- Spend on curtailment modeling exists on the sponsor side (Google paid for Aurora).

Not found, and this is the central gap:
- Any RFP, lender policy, rating criterion, forum complaint or current spend that buys a backup-generator legal-runway analysis. A KBRA data center CMBS release reportedly says it reviewed third-party engineering, environmental and appraisal reports, with no power or curtailment report named [U: search summary; release not opened]. KBRA's data center ABS methodology exists but sits behind a login ([KBRA](https://www.kbra.com/publications/ywsVHsMw/abs-data-center-abs-global-rating-methodology) [U]). Data center ABS commentary discusses tenant credit and leases, not power ([datacentres.com](https://www.datacentres.com/news/data-centre-abs-issuance-hits-38b-as-wall-street-securitizes-the-ai-lease-boom-slot1-2026-09-01) [S]). Commentary on CoreWeave's loans stresses contract-tenor mismatch and collateral value ([Global Data Center Hub](https://www.globaldatacenterhub.com/p/coreweaves-85b-quarter-when-gpu-debt) [S]).
- The weakest link in the Phase I analogy: Phase I reports are bought because they establish a statutory CERCLA defense under "all appropriate inquiries", which EPA recognized for ASTM E1527-21 from Feb 13, 2023 ([Spencer Fane](https://www.spencerfane.com/insight/astms-2021-update-to-the-phase-i-standard-now-satisfies-all-appropriate-inquiry) [S]). A curtailment report has no safe harbor. It sells only if credit committees or rating agencies make it a condition. Most of the big dollars are hyperscaler-tenant deals where lenders price the tenant, so the real segment is smaller: spec, powered land and unrated neocloud loans.

## 4. Competitors and incumbents

Direct (lender-facing power-curtailment or permit-runway report): none found. Caveat: search-engine summaries, not exhaustive proof.

| Player | What it is | Funding / traction | Threat |
|---|---|---|---|
| GridCARE | AI mapping of hidden grid capacity for data center and grid operators | $64M Series A May 2026 (Sutter Hill), $77.5M total, $13.5M seed 2025; freed 80 MW at PGE ([DCD](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/gridcare-raises-64m-in-series-a-funding-round/) [U]) | Medium. Has the data and the cash; customer is the developer, not the lender |
| Voltus | PJM demand response aggregator, "bring your own capacity" | $225M Series D Oct 8, 2026; Google up to 100 MW ([Voltus](https://www.voltus.co/press/voltus-google-bring-your-own-capacity-pjm), parent file); 20 GW goal by 2030 ([Latitude](https://www.latitudemedia.com/news/voltus-raises-225-million-to-scale-byoc-for-data-centers/) [S]) | Low as competitor; sells MW, conflicted. Possible referral partner |
| Aurora Energy Research, Modo Energy | Independent curtailment and PJM analytics | Aurora paid by Google; Modo claims a 500 MW site could run diesel "up to 417 hours" at $325/MW-day ([Modo](https://modoenergy.com/research/pjm-data-center-demand-growth-non-capacity-backed-load-reliability) [V]) | Medium. Could add the exposure-distribution layer |
| Enverus | Siting analytics; claims 250+ financial institution customers on its Canadian page ([Enverus](https://enverus.com/canada)) [V]; data center siting page: [Enverus](https://www.enverus.com/segments/data-center/) | Established analytics vendor | Medium-high. Existing lender relationships |

Conflicted for lender work, but could white-label |

## 5. Bottom-up market size (inference, assumptions stated)

- Tracked public GPU, neocloud and AI-campus financings: 41 in 2025 and 50 in 2026 through Oct 10, $231B total ([AmCompute](https://www.amcompute.com/gpu-financing-tracker) [V]). Private and bilateral loans are not counted; assume 1-2x more, so 120-180 a year globally, close to the founder's 150.

- Price is not the obstacle: $20-45k is under 0.01% of a $2B financing. The obstacle is whether it is required.
- Cost (my estimate): 25-50 professional hours (engineer plus air attorney) at $250-500 blended is $6-25k per first-time campus report, so gross margin on a $25k report ranges 0-75%. The "same permit dataset serves every report" claim only helps for repeat markets.

The dossier covers HGR and data-export rules but misses the 2026 crackdown on foreign due-diligence activity. China's Regulations on Industrial and Supply Chain Security took effect 31 Mar 2026. Article 13 restricts 'information gathering' on supply chains, and the countermeasures include limits on cooperating with Chinese partners and travel or residence limits on individuals. Precedent: Mintz was fined about $1.5M and ordered to stop 'foreign-related statistical investigations' in 2023, and Bain and Capvision were raided or questioned. On 5 Aug 2026 MOFCOM put 6-7 US due-diligence firms on its Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law countermeasure list. Caveat: that listing was tied to Xinjiang forced-labor sanctions, not pharma, and the sources disagree on the count. My inference is that the BIOSECURE 'ownership chain' and 'supply-chain mapping' product is the same genre of activity. Chinese licensors control data-room access and have a reason to refuse a vendor that markets itself as an arm of US list enforcement. Bilingual scientists working inside China carry personal risk. Scientists working outside China depend on the seller clearing HGR, PIPL and CAC transfers, which the dossier says can take months. The only workable version is staged, seller-consented and US-based, which is not the product as written.

The liability asymmetry makes the product hard to sell at the stated price. A $25-70k memo sits against $77-172M average upfronts, and the idea's own example deals carry $400M or more. Liability would be capped near the fee, and no E&O pricing or case law was found (dossier gap). Kovel-style privilege requires counsel to retain the consultant for legal advice, so the 'sits under privilege' pitch is weak for commercial diligence. Buyers' counsel will either demand real reliance, which a 3-4 person shop cannot insure, or treat the memo as non-reliance color. The dossier concedes that a paper review would catch an Elevar-type facility gap but not a KBP-type concealment, which is the failure that destroys value. Deal teams are buying blame transfer more than information, and blame transfer comes from ICON, Big-4 firms and law-firm-retained experts, not a startup. Third-party reliance law (foreseeable-recipient negligent misrepresentation) also means a memo that is passed to co-investors or a licensor expands exposure beyond the fee.

The 'GAP' competition verdict is wrong, and the window is filling now. Vision Lifesciences markets exactly this: data integrity and GCP audit-trail checks with source-document spot checks, a CMC tech-transfer audit, and a 'Technical Data Room' for HGRAC compliance. I confirmed this on its page. It lists no pricing, named clients or team credentials, so it is weak but present. ICON has a published case study on an Asia-Pacific licensor with a thin data room: it flagged CMC risks and costed the non-clinical and clinical work needed for regulators, which is the Western-format gap memo. Alacrita has a case study doing tox, Phase 1/2 and CMC diligence on a China-origin in-license, plus seller-side 'DD readiness'. Zamann Pharma published a July 2026 piece on whether US pharma can verify China CMC evidence. Independent consultants are advertising NMPA-to-FDA CTD gap and translation verification. What remains is the dossier's own estimate of about 15-25 platforms and a $1.5-4M annual pool. That pool is a thin-margin boutique that needs named, FDA-experienced bilingual scientists and law-firm introductions before the first dollar, with no moat except a track record that does not yet exist.

Deal volume is hostage to unresolved US policy, so the pool can shrink or be absorbed into counsel-led compliance. The Sept 2025 draft EO to put China licensing under CFIUS review was denied but never closed. BINSA was introduced in the House on 12 Jun 2026 (H.R. 9102) and in the Senate on 6 Aug 2026 (S. 5316). It would put licensing from covered Chinese persons under Treasury review; one summary says an outright bar, which I could not verify. COINS final regulations are due 13 Mar 2027, and whether biotech is designated is described as the most consequential open question. Reuters reported on 18 Sep 2026 that Treasury is weighing a loose rule restricting only pathogen or weaponizable work, with nothing expected before the Trump-Xi meeting. The why-now is weaker than the finalist file claims. BIOSECURE's Dec 18, 2026 list is a date, not a spend event. I found no documented FDA refusal of China preclinical GLP data, and the dossier also found none. Pharaon claims 20+ US INDs on its data. 'FDA-acceptability' is therefore a rhetorical pain today, not a demonstrated one.

objections: The revenue engine is sized on household counts that no real developer program comes close to. The model needs about 3,000 enrolled households (1-3 mile radius) to reach the claimed $1M+ per program. Every actual developer neighbor program found covers a tiny radius. Festus, MO (CRG) offers a buyout to the 12 nearest homes, raised in June 2026 from FMV+10% to FMV+15% plus a $10k moving allowance. Mason County, WV (Nscale) covers 53 homes. Howell Twp, MI covers 1,000 ft. DeForest, WI (QTS draft) covered 1/4 mile. At the idea's own prices ($300 per household, 1% per year of a $3-5k-per-home escrow, $1,500 per claim), 12 homes is about $3.6k of enrollment revenue and 53 homes is about $16k plus roughly $2k per year. Even the 300-home pilot in the 30-day plan is only about $90k enrollment plus $10k per year, before one state counsel opinion, the price-effect model, appraisers and claims staff. The only 4,500-household example (NorthPoint, Hazle) was a lump-sum check, not a guarantee, and that project was rejected on zoning grounds. The realistic market is tens of thousands of dollars per deal, which is a consulting practice and not a $1M+ per program business.

No evidence that the buyer pays for this product, and the revealed preference is buyouts. The Federation of American Scientists report 'Before Breaking Ground' analyzes ten executed developer-municipality agreements. Zero contain a property-value guarantee. The only neighbor-home mechanism in any of the ten is Festus's developer-run voluntary buyout, and a lawsuit alleges it forces owners to use a developer-approved appraiser. Every developer action found is a buyout run in-house with 'highest of three valuations' (Mason County), not a neutral third-party guarantee. Buyouts give the developer something a guarantee does not: the homes become employee and contractor housing (Mason), the nearest opponents disappear, and the payout is certain. A guarantee only helps owners who later sell. The dossier's own gap list admits it found no RFP, county ordinance, paid pilot or developer offering a value guarantee. Two other results are bad signs. Money did not buy approval or trust: Hazle residents refused the $10k checks, and Festus residents sued even after the council approved the project 6-2. Sabey won its Indianapolis variances with a commissioned study, not a guarantee, so the guarantee is not a gating item for approval. That makes willingness to pay low and urgency lower.

The history of this exact product is zero claims and no one using it. The 2011 Poletti & Associates conference deck (a wind-farm property-value appraiser, primary source, text extracted) says Lee County, IL's guarantee plan for Mendota Ridge had a 5-year limit, no owner ever used it, and the county declined to renew. It lists the problems: it benefits only owners who sell, it is hard to administer, the county ends up administering it by default, there are multiple appraisals, and there are disputes over who hires the appraiser and over what loss is guaranteed. It concludes the data show 'no real problem that needs to be solved' and names annual participation payments as the simpler alternative. This creates a pricing trap. If the guarantee is cheap because nobody claims, the developer will not prepay $300 per household plus 1% of escrow per year for a symbolic gesture and will settle claims ad hoc with a local appraiser. If claims are real, the payouts are far larger than the idea assumes. The dossier's own model puts expected payout at $3.8-5.4k per household against a $3-5k escrow, several times the idea's assumption of 10-30%. A 10% deductible fixes the developer's cost but guts what residents asked for. The Hazle resident's complaint was about value loss, not about losses beyond the first 10%.

Insurance classification is a gating legal risk, and the idea's economic advantage is exactly the feature that triggers it. I read the NY DFS General Counsel opinion (OGC 08-07-31) directly. A plan that pays homeowners money on a sale below a covered value is insurance under Ins. Law 1101(a) and prohibited financial guaranty insurance under 6901(a)(1)(D). The drivers were payment only on sales below value (indemnity on the specific home), a valuation index built from appraisals and sales, and administrator discretion over claims. The only structure counsel distinguished as permissible pays solely on index performance regardless of the owner's actual gain or loss, with no administrator discretion. For this idea that would mean paying every household, which is the $10k-check economics it claims to beat. The developer-as-obligor argument is untested, and the dossier found no state-by-state analysis and no named permissible structure. Each state needs its own opinion (tens of thousands of dollars each), and any one adverse regulator or county attorney ends a deal. The dossier also notes some states restrict BPOs, which would raise valuation cost above the $300 assumption in those states.

Go-to-market: wrong co-signer, wrong timing, wrong cost-to-serve. (a) The county cannot or will not be the backstop. A county-hired consultant in Delaware County, IN called property-value guarantees 'largely unenforceable by county officials' and 'uncommon', and the plan commission removed them in 2023. In St. Joseph County, IN, where guarantees were imposed on solar, the design is a surety bond (20% of assessed value within one mile) plus a developer-funded assessor with no neutral startup, a developer said it would 'look elsewhere', and commissioners cannot veto the ordinance. Where guarantees are mandated, developers meet them with a bond and an appraiser or avoid the county. Where voluntary, they pick buyouts. (b) The sales cycle is long and the revenue is contingent on project approval. DeForest's staff met QTS for about seven months, the draft deal died three weeks after announcement, Greeley's pre-annexation agreement ran 18 months, and Pikeville's MOU ran 120 days plus a 60-day extension. The idea's 90-day gate to a signed pilot is unrealistic. Fee revenue starts only at development-agreement signing, and Data Center Watch counted 45-75 projects per quarter blocked or delayed, so a large share of prospects never close. (c) The reference value freezes at first public disclosure, but site selection runs through shell LLCs and NDAs (NBC found this in a majority of 30+ proposals in 14 states), so the vendor must be inside before the public announcement. The 30-day plan instead cold-calls developers that have already gone public. (d) A 10-year contingent obligation sits poorly with the developer's exit. Developers build to sell or refinance into a thin stabilized-asset market (CBRE: about 7% of investors target stabilized assets), so a CFO will see an encumbrance on the asset, and counsel will push the obligation onto a bank or fund administrator. That turns the startup into a sub-vendor to Epiq, Kroll or a bank trust desk, priced at fund-administration rates (the dossier's weak source: $150-500 per disbursement versus the idea's $1,500 per claim). My conclusion on this last point is inference.

Price-effect evidence cuts against urgency, and the moat is thin. Developers' standard defense is studies showing no average effect: Realtor.com's 43-ZIP match, George Mason, the Sabey/Integra study, and a Texas analysis. A developer who believes them has little reason to pre-fund an escrow, and a developer who does not believe them faces the payout math in objection 3. Valuation is also weakest where the programs would sit. Vendor sources put AVM median error at 10-15% or more in thin rural markets versus 3-5% urban, and one academic result cited in the snippet found about 25% of rural properties appraised more than 5% above contract price versus 12.7% urban, so the frozen reference and the control index are noisy exactly in exurban sites. That noise creates disputes and false payouts, and the dossier's 'only arithmetic, no causation argument' pitch is weaker than it sounds. Stated moat: the price-effect model and county relationships, but the mechanics are copyable by title, escrow and fund-administration firms that already hold the deed data and the bank relationships. The price-effect evidence kills the buyer from both directions, and the paper that matters is not in the dossier. A UC Berkeley Energy Institute working paper (Schlauch and Greenhill, Sept 2026, not peer-reviewed) uses a matched stacked event study, which is essentially this idea's control index. It finds large data centers cut housing values 3% on average within 3 miles and 7.2% within 1 mile. The decline persists for 5+ years and is larger for hyperscale facilities, urban sites and the first data center in an area. For recent projects the effect is capitalized almost entirely at announcement. (a) If that is right, the guarantee pays out on the mean, not the tail. The escrow of $3-5k per household is undersized, and a baseline frozen at 'first public disclosure' is either already contaminated by leaks or hit immediately after the freeze. Any developer who reads the paper will refuse to be obligor. (b) If it is wrong (Realtor.com's 43 matched ZIPs, George Mason, Integra), the developer's incumbent answer is to commission a 'no impact' appraisal and win. Align did this at Coal City, IL (LaSalle Appraisal Group). Sabey did this in Indianapolis, with the commission approving on 18 March 2026 and no guarantee offered. They fund community packages themselves (Meta's $1B fund, Microsoft's Community-First pledge) and want the PR for themselves, not a third-party index that publishes a number against them. The independents who would outsource are the small-effect projects that least need it. In every precedent, the sponsor was compelled to buy the administrator: contamination class-action settlements (Almon v. McWane, Anniston) and Norfolk Southern after its derailment. Berkeley says the effect is highly localized (about 1 mile), so a county will restrict eligibility to a ring of hundreds of homes, as in Mason (53), not 3,000. Revenue scales down to roughly $100-300k, not $1M+. The role is also ministerial: the county writes the formula into the development agreement, a trust bank holds the escrow, and a three-appraiser panel handles disputes (the Mason norm, Illinois HB4319's design, and NS's approved-appraiser model). Illinois HB4319 has shown no movement since referral to Rules on 1/14/2026, so there is no legislative forcing function. Layered on the dossier's own gating risks (NY DFS treating pay-on-sale as financial guaranty insurance; no buyer, RFP or paid pilot found), the 90-day signed-pilot gate is unrealistic.

Pre-mortem (2028 cause of death, most likely first): (1) no independent developer will be obligor of record once counsel and the Berkeley numbers are in front of them, so the company never gets a signed escrow. (2) The few counties that do adopt a rider hand the administrator role to an incumbent (A&M, Epiq, a trust bank plus appraisal panel) via RFP or because the developer's law firm already knows them. (3) The startup is left selling control-index research that Berkeley and Realtor.com give away. Of the three, only (3) is fixable by pivoting. The venture-scale version of the idea is close to dead on competition and incumbent response alone. What survives is a small services practice, probably as a subcontractor or white-label partner to a VAP administrator rather than a rival.

(4) A voluntary pre-approval guarantee anywhere (wind, transmission or data center) with meaningful claim volume that was not driven by moral hazard. (5) A county ordinance that names the startup's control index as the standard of record, which would give a real standard-setter position that A&M cannot copy quickly.

objections: REGULATION (gating): the product is the exact thing insurance regulators have already ruled on, and every ruling I found goes one way. NY DFS OGC 08-07-31 held a pay-on-sale home-value plan is insurance and is financial guaranty insurance NY does not permit, so it cannot be sold there at all. NY DFS OGC 11-07-02 went further: it reversed an earlier opinion that had cleared a nonprofit index program, reasoning that a payment tied to a decline in the homeowner's own property value is a fortuitous event, and that selling it without an insurer licence is doing an insurance business. This idea's trigger (net sale price of the specific house vs a control-index-adjusted reference) is more tied to the individual home than the ZIP-index triggers in those opinions, so it looks more insurance-like, not less. The dossier's 'developer is obligor, so not insurance' defence is untested, and the 2011 opinion's fortuity reasoning did not turn on who pays. A second licensing trap sits on the administrator: NY treats any discretionary claim determination as 'adjusting' needing an independent adjuster licence, and NAIC says 30+ states licence adjusters/TPAs. The calculation agent decides arm's-length status, 60-day listing compliance and disputes, which is discretion. One adverse state opinion also kills the county's ability to approve the rider in that state. This is 50-state legal work before the first dollar, and the 90-day gate does not allow for it.

ECONOMICS AND TRACK RECORD OF THE EXACT MECHANISM: the closest real-world analog was tried and nobody used it. Lee County, IL's wind-farm guarantee (Mendota Ridge) used the same design (appraise as-if-no-project, reappraise at sale, company covers the shortfall). Per the appraiser who ran the analysis, 'No property owner ever used the plan' and the county declined to renew it. His list of problems reads like this idea's roadmap: it only benefits sellers, is hard to administer, the county ends up administering it, multiple appraisals with disputes over who hires the appraiser, confusion over what loss is guaranteed, and it can depress prices beyond the project area. His recommended alternative is annual participation payments, which are simpler and avoid disputes (i.e. a recurring check, the thing this idea is meant to beat). This sets up a bimodal trap. If claims are rare, as in Lee County, residents and counties see no value, will not renew, and the claim-fee revenue ($1,500 per sale) never appears. If claims are frequent, the escrow drains: the dossier's own estimate is about $3.8-5.4k expected payout per household against a $3-5k escrow without a deductible. 'Cheaper than $10k checks and more credible' only holds if payouts are rare, and payouts being rare is exactly when residents decide it is worthless. A 10% deductible fixes the economics by making the benefit smaller still. The ask side is also mismatched: a Lysander, NY committee's CBA suggestion list asks for an escrow equal to 20% of the value of nearby residential properties (about $60k on a $300k house), 12-20x the $3-5k per household assumed. Residents anchoring on 20% means either the developer pays several times the budgeted amount or residents judge the program undersized.
