A buyout solves the developer's problem (buffer, land assembly, ends the liability, homes become worker housing) and gives the neighbor what an adjacent owner wants, which is out. A guarantee leaves the developer with a 10-year contingent liability and the neighbor still next to the site. Owners close enough to be seriously worried take the buyout; owners far enough to stay have little loss to insure, so the guarantee is left serving the middle ring with the weakest need. No developer has offered a value guarantee and I found no RFP, ordinance or county asking for a neutral administrator. The wins where value was disputed (Sabey, Decatur Township, IN) came from commissioned studies, not guarantees. The idea needs a developer to volunteer a 10-year pre-committed payout that its counsel may read as an admission, in a market where cheaper rhetorical substitutes (a study, a check, a buyout) work. Property value is also one ask among dozens in these negotiations (utilities, water, infrastructure, jobs, schools), and Gallup-via-secondary reporting puts resource strain at 50% of opponents' reasons, utility bills 15%, and quality of life or property value combined at 22%.

TIMING, SALES CYCLE AND MARKET SIZE: the why-now is a moratorium-and-opposition story, which shrinks the paying buyer pool rather than expanding it. Projects are dying or shrinking before a rider matters (Hazle rejected on zoning, DeForest collapsed three weeks after being announced, Festus scaled back). Hyperscaler capex growth is forecast to decelerate (UBS: 76% in 2026, 25% in 2027, 6% in 2028), with financing strain flagged; the target customer, the independent developer, is the most financing-fragile and is typically a project SPV that will be sold or flipped inside a 10-year obligation, so counterparty credit forces a bank or Epiq-class administrator in as obligor-of-record, which turns the startup into a subcontractor to someone else's balance sheet. Revenue only starts when a county puts a rider in a development agreement and the escrow is funded at signing. DeForest staff spent about 7 months with the developer before announcement, so a signed pilot in 90 days is unrealistic and 12-24 months to first cash is more plausible. The dossier's own sizing is $4-10M a year at 5-10% capture of about 240 contested projects, a services business. Illinois HB4319, cited as a credible threat that could create a safe-harbor market, was referred to the Rules Committee on 1/14/2026 with no later action found, and the '1.5x fair market value' term in the dossier did not verify. On 7 Powers there is no durable power: the mechanics are copyable, Pennsylvania's NDA ban means terms are public, the FAS, Columbia and Franklin County materials are free templates, the Columbia piece shows property-value guarantees are already a standard CBA clause that law firms draft, and Epiq, title firms and banks already hold the neutrality, escrow and closing-table access.

DATA AND VALUATION FOUNDATION IS WEAKEST WHERE THE PRODUCT IS SOLD: the idea says 'public sale records, no sensors', but about 9-12 states do not disclose sale prices (Texas, Utah, Idaho, Montana, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alaska, North Dakota, plus others by list). Several are major build-out states, and Texas is named in the idea's own pilot plan. In those states prices come only via MLS feeds that can't be republished, and off-MLS sales (FSBO, family transfers, cash deals) are invisible, so the trigger needs claimant-supplied closing statements and a verification process, which is claims adjudication, not 'arithmetic' (and feeds back into the adjuster-licensing problem). The whole contract rests on a frozen reference value from an AVM plus BPO, and AVM accuracy is weakest in thin rural markets: vendors publish 2.7-2.9% median error nationally but no rural breakdown, and academic work finds appraisal bias is worse in rural areas (about 25% of rural properties appraised more than 5% above contract price vs 12.7% urban). The median 2026 data center sits about 27 miles out in areas with about 70% fewer housing units per square mile, so the control index is built on very few repeat sales. Any reference-value error becomes a payout, since the product is a put option on one house. Baseline error plus 12-15% idiosyncratic price noise is what the dossier already says drains the escrow. 'First public disclosure' as the baseline date is also contestable after months of confidential land assembly. Finally, the administrator is paid by the developer, the same developer-pays defect the parent research used to dismiss consultancies (Meta's Newton County study was disbelieved). County co-approval mitigates this but the neutrality moat is asserted, not demonstrated.

result.what_would_change_my_mind:
Any one of these would move me from 'serious' toward 'manageable'.

1. A written signal that a lender will pay. A credit-committee memo, term sheet or closing-condition draft from a data center debt originator, lender counsel or technical advisor naming power-runway analysis, or a paid pilot (not a free report) on a live deal at $15k or more from an institution that has to make it a condition. Three of 15 saying 'we would consider it' does not count.
2. A rating-agency hook. A Moody's, KBRA, Fitch or S&P analyst confirming that backup-generation permit limits will be a disclosure or stress item in a methodology or presale report. That would play the role Phase I's regulatory standard plays.
3. A legal opinion. An air attorney's written view that PJM- or ERCOT-directed generator use at EEA1 or at a curtailment trigger is non-emergency operation under 40 CFR 63.6640(f) and the state permit, and that DOE 202(c) orders do not routinely override the permit cap. That would turn the legal-runway analysis into a durable product rather than a contested opinion.
4. Market-timing facts. FERC accepting IRAS substantially as filed, and ERCOT finalizing its SB 6 backup-generation trigger. Together with a documented count of 40+ financings a year where the lender carries power risk and the campus relies on diesel emergency engines, rather than gas turbines or tenant-priced credit, that would validate the $10M-class market.
5. A fee benchmark. Two lenders' technical advisors or lender counsel saying they would buy rather than build this, at a price that clears roughly 60% gross margin after liability cover.
6. Independence clarified. A structure that drops the cross-sell of the permit-modification service to graded campuses, with the lost revenue still leaving a viable business.

Short of that, the cheapest decisive test is two or three calls to lender counsel and technical advisors asking one question: 'Has this ever appeared on a closing checklist, and who paid for it?' If the answer is 'never', the idea is not yet a business.

objections: The legal premise fails in the scenario the report sells. The pitch says a campus curtailed for 200 hours is legally uncovered after 100. But in a real grid emergency, federal law now says the opposite. EPA's Jan 26, 2026 data-center guidance, quoted in DOE's Feb 4, 2026 rehearing order, says operation under a DOE 202(c) order is emergency operation with no limit on emergency engine use, and those hours do not count toward the 50-hour non-emergency allowance. DOE's order adds that FPA 202(c)(3) shields compliance with any environmental limit on hours of operation. DOE has used this repeatedly in 2026: ERCOT in January, PJM in January, May 18-20, June 30 and July 14-21. PJM's own Aug 6 deck shows 20 plants and 23 units running above permit limits under the waiver, for 692 hours (unit-owner data, power plants, not data-center engines). Texas SB 2321 separately lets TCEQ waive enforcement of emissions limits for on-site backup generation when ERCOT asks. A lender can reasonably conclude that the government clears permit caps whenever EEA3 is near. The dossier filed 202(c) as a 'counter-force'. It is closer to the whole ballgame. What remains is non-emergency curtailment under PJM's new IRAS service. That is still pending at FERC, starts June 1, 2027 at the earliest, and applies only to new 50 MW+ loads that did not bring capacity. It also fires before pre-emergency load management, with compensation. EPA keeps issuing program-by-program letters that widen the 50-hour allowance (NRG, June 24, 2026). So the report's core legal conclusion has a half-life of weeks. One new DOE order or EPA letter flips a 'fail' to a 'pass' after the lender has already relied on it.

No evidence that anyone will pay, and the timing makes revenue unlikely before 2027-28. The dossier found no lender policy, RFP, rating criterion or current spend. The Phase I analogy lacks the thing that makes Phase I mandatory, a statutory safe harbor. Lenders' counsel already run power diligence in-house (Davis Polk says once power diligence is satisfied it is 'standard project-on-project risk'). The Bracewell data-center finance guide I fetched says nothing about generators or curtailment reports. A curtailment report becomes a credit term only after FERC rules on IRAS, and FERC on Sept 29 suspended the companion backstop procurement to Feb 28, 2027. The segment where lenders carry power risk without an investment-grade tenant is the one in retreat. Lenders are balking at neocloud debt and Nvidia is asking insurers to backstop it. CoreWeave's debt is $35B and subject to the 'refinancing wall' narrative. The buyer pool is narrowest where the product is most relevant. The dossier's own bottom-up is $1.5-6M a year, versus the pitch's $10M, for a business that needs lawyer-grade people on every deliverable.

The product as designed is structurally awkward to deliver legally and commercially. The report is a legal interpretation of air permits, authored by a non-law firm and 'co-signed' by a retained air attorney. State bar opinions treat a lawyer ratifying non-lawyer work, or sharing fees with the non-lawyer company, as unauthorized-practice and Rule 5.4 problems. The sources I found are old and state-specific and not on all fours, but the risk pattern is clear, and a legal opinion mixed with a consulting product will be examined by lender counsel. The borrower pays, and the borrower supplies the run logs, fuel inventory and telemetry the report depends on. That recreates the issuer-pays conflict the report's 'independence' pitch claims to avoid. A wrong 'pass' invites a reliance claim. That means E&O cover, liability caps and reliance letters, none of which a new entrant has. The dossier's own cost estimate (25-50 professional hours at $250-500) gives 0-75% gross margin on a $25k report. Independent engineers and law firms (the proposed channel) can do this in-house and keep the margin once the template exists.

The data is fragmented, so there is no standardized product and no data moat. 'Per-engine hour caps' do not generalize. Many Texas data-center generators sit under permit-by-rule 106.511 with sitewide fuel limits, where run hours are only an alternative limit, and PBR carries no public notice. Virginia uses pooled and total-hour caps (500 hours; the dossier's example of a 3,000-hour pool across 50 engines). Each state differs, so every report is bespoke permit archaeology. The public pieces are already public: Virginia DEQ posts data-center air permits, and journalists and NGOs (Technical.ly, Sierra Club, Public Citizen) have mapped them. The non-public pieces are not available to a third party. PJM's large-load registry is restricted to commissions, utilities, the market monitor and FERC. SB 6 disclosures run from utility to ERCOT with no public route in the text. EPA's July 7, 2026 proposal would remove public participation from minor-source permitting, which would shrink even the public record. 'The same permit dataset serves every report' is false when most of the work is site-specific and depends on operator-provided data.

The fallback being underwritten is shrinking, and the exposed campuses are the least bankable. Large new campuses are going behind-the-meter gas for prime power, not relying on diesel backup. INNIO booked a 1.1 GW order for BTM prime power in July 2026, its S-1/A projects BTM and hybrid at 50-60% of incremental data-center demand by 2030, and Abilene-style gas builds are cited as the model. PJM's IRAS only reaches new loads that fail to bring their own capacity, so campuses with their own supply are not curtailable at all. Virginia HB 507 now requires Tier 4-level controls for new permits, which changes the engine fleet. A diesel-only fallback is therefore the profile of the weakest, least-financeable projects. Gas prime-power permitting (Title V/PSD, no 100-hour concept) is a different and harder product from the one pitched. The 'bad score becomes an inbound lead for the dual-mode permit service' flywheel relies on the same shaky legal ground in objection 1.

result.title: Home Equity Assurance for Data Center Neighbors (refined, demoted to a watch item)
result.one_liner: As pitched (developer-funded, third-party-administered 10-year home-value guarantee, about $1M a program) it is dead; the strongest survivor is an independent, published-method property-value review sold to counties and paid by the applicant, with a deductible guarantee rider only on large-ring sites.
result.pitch:
Verdict: not a venture. The original pitch fails on evidence. Every 2026 developer move on the home-value fear is a buyout, a put-to-developer or a check, and ten executed agreements reviewed by a critic contained no value guarantee. Alvarez & Marsal already runs court-tested value assurance programs (Norfolk Southern's pays market value minus sale price below 95% of appraiser-determined unaffected value). Berkeley Energy Institute WP 366 (Sept 2026, not peer reviewed) finds -3% within 3 miles and -7.2% within 1 mile, capitalized at announcement, so a guarantee with no deductible costs about $5-10k of escrow per home, the same as the $10k checks it was meant to beat.

What survives is narrower. An independent, published-method price-effect review, selected by the county and paid through the applicant-funded review escrow, plus a draft rider with a 10% deductible. A guarantee is offered only on large-ring sites (500 to 5,000 homes) where buyouts are impossible and checks drew bribery backlash. With the deductible, expected cost is roughly $1-4k per enrolled home, so the rider is affordable.

Realistic revenue is $190-210k in year one for an 800-home program, then $50-70k a year, with 12 to 24 months to first cash and state counsel opinions up front. That is a consulting practice with an option on a future mandate and an exit as white-label valuation supplier to VAP administrators. It is not worth the founder's focus unless the two-week test finds three live matters with a named budget owner. Revive only on a signed LOI for 1,000+ homes at $150k+, a county or state mandate naming a neutral administrator, or a written subcontract offer from A&M, Epiq or Kroll.
result.wedge_customer: If revived: independent (non-hyperscale) developers on suburban or exurban sites with roughly 500-5,000 homes inside a 1-3 mile ring, where a buyout is infeasible and a lump-sum check drew bribery coverage. Entry is through county attorneys and the land-use counsel who draft the development agreement (they take calls and decide structure), not developer GCs cold. Hyperscalers (self-fund, want the PR) and small buyout rings of 12-53 homes are excluded.
result.first_product: An independent, county-selected, applicant-funded property-value impact review using a published method (matched event-study or control index), delivered with a draft development-agreement rider that has a ring, a 10% deductible and a three-appraiser dispute panel. Guarantee administration is only sold after a signed rider and a state counsel view that it is not insurance. No sensors, no obligor role, no escrow held by us.
result.pricing: Payer is the developer, through the county's applicant-funded review escrow. Review: $10-40k flat. Guarantee program, re-priced: $40-75k set-up, $100-150 per enrolled household, 0.75-1% of escrow per year, $750-1,500 per adjudicated claim (mostly panel pass-through). 800-home program: about $190-210k year one, $50-70k a year after, about $0.6-0.8M over ten years. The $300 per household, $1,500 claim fee and float income lines are dropped. Escrow is sized at $3.5k per home with a 10% deductible; without one it must be $5-10k.
result.why_now: Real for the problem, weak for the product. Kept: Berkeley WP 366 (10 Sept 2026) gives the first national causal estimate, so negotiations now have a number for ring and deductible; NorthPoint's lump-sum checks drew bribery backlash; 108 ZIPs now host a large data center, up from 12 in 2015. Dropped: NY and Texas pauses (grid and water actions that shrink the buyer pool) and Illinois HB4319 (stalled in Rules since 1/14/2026). The same 2026 conditions produced buyouts, not guarantees.
result.moat: None of Helmer's 7 Powers is reachable in 12 months. Counter-positioning fails because A&M already earns from value assurance programs. Cornered resource fails because deeds, MLS and AVMs are public and WP 366 makes the method reproducible. Scale, network and switching costs do not exist for one-off programs. The only reachable position is standard-setter status: an open methodology that a county ordinance or statute names as the standard of record. That requires giving the method away, so it fits a research practice and not a software business, and a Big Four-class advisory firm can match a first track record within a quarter.
result.bottom_up_market: About 240 contested projects a year (Data Center Watch Q1 and Q2 2026, annualized) x guarantee-compatible subset of 5-10% (large ring, independent developer, no buyout path) = 12-24 programs a year. Early capture of 10-30% = 1-5 programs x about $200k first-year revenue = $0.2-1.0M a year at best, in years 2-3, and $0 until a first signed rider. Option D reviews add 10-20 a year x $15-30k = $0.15-0.6M at services margins. Ceiling is low single-digit millions a year. No paying customer has been found anywhere, and the large-ring subset size is my guess.
result.competitors_and_edge: Alvarez & Marsal runs productized Value Assurance Programs (verified: administrator of Norfolk Southern's East Palestine VAP, interim Sept 2023 to Aug 2026, long-term to Aug 2031), with a court-tested template, GIS, outreach and a real-estate economics practice. Epiq, Kroll and JND have neutrality and bank relationships but no valuation models. Developers buy commissioned no-impact studies (Align/LaSalle at Coal City, Sabey/Integra in Indianapolis). Berkeley, Realtor.com, GMU and NAR publish the research free; Columbia and FAS publish free CBA templates. Edge left: a data-center-specific published control-index method and a price point below A&M for sub-500-home programs. Neither is defensible against an incumbent that decides to serve the segment.
result.riskiest_assumption: Someone with authority and budget (a developer, a county, or the land-use counsel drafting the development agreement) will put a third-party-administered pay-on-sale value guarantee for a ring of 500+ homes into a real agreement, at a total fee of $100k+, instead of a buyout, bond, check or commissioned study. All three critiques converge on this, and public evidence already leans against it: zero guarantees in ten executed agreements, buyouts everywhere, no RFP or ordinance naming an administrator.
result.two_week_test: 14 days, about 15-20 founder hours, $0. Days 1-3 (desk): list 30 live matters with a vote in the next 6 months and a documented public ask for property-value protection (Lysander NY, St. Joseph and Delaware IN, Festus, Mason, Coal City, Howell, Hazle, Decatur, Dowagiac). Record ring size, developer offer, who administers, who pays. Days 3-12: 20 thirty-minute interviews, honestly as a student researcher: 8 county attorneys and planners, 6 land-use or real-estate counsel who draft development agreements, 3 independent developers' community-affairs staff, 2 bank trust or escrow officers, 1 ex-VAP appraiser or economist. Ask current-state questions first, then show a one-page term sheet (1-mile ring, 10% deductible, $3.5k escrow per home, $40-75k set-up) and ask: why not a buyout, bond or study; who owns this budget; will you read a 2-page draft rider. Pre-registered pass: at least 3 of 20 name a live matter with a guarantee on the table, no administrator in place and a named budget owner, plus at least 1 written agreement to read the rider. Kill: 0-1 live matters, most say buyout, bond or study, or A&M is already on the matter. If fewer than 5 of 40 outreach attempts are answered, log it as no access, a finding about the founder's ability to sell this and not about demand.
result.how_critiques_were_addressed: Critique 1 (serious, A&M, Berkeley, buyouts, thin slice): conceded A&M and the Berkeley miss. I verified both directly: the Norfolk Southern VAP page names A&M, and WP 366's abstract gives -3% within 3 miles and -7.2% within 1 mile, capitalized at announcement. Re-priced revenue to $100-300k a program, dropped the HB4319 and moratoria why-now, and conceded no moat. Pushed back only on the claim that counties cannot tell bluffers apart (a funded escrow is a costly signal), which leaves adverse selection in who signs as the real issue. Critique 2 (fatal, household count, no buyer, zero-claims history, insurance, GTM): conceded revenue arithmetic, revealed preference for buyouts (zero guarantees in ten executed agreements) and the unrealistic 90-day gate; partly pushed back on insurance, because the verified Norfolk Southern VAP is a defendant-funded third-party pay-on-sale shortfall program, so the NY opinions look structure- and state-specific rather than a category ban. The deductible becomes mandatory, which cuts what residents asked for. Net: the dossier's own kill triggers 3 (buyouts preferred) and part of 1 (insurance) are already met by public evidence, and two of the three pre-mortem causes (no obligor, incumbent takes the administrator role) cannot be fixed by the company. Hence alive=false, with one revive path: pass the two-week test, a signed LOI, a mandate or an incumbent subcontract. result.title: Stranded-Loan Cure Desk (formerly Finish Crew)
result.one_liner: A cure desk for credit unions and community banks holding stranded pre-PTO solar loans: triage each loan into cure or unwind, then manage the cure through a licensed contractor-of-record partner for a flat per-file fee, with free panel enrollment done before the next installer fails. A small services business, not a venture, and it survives only if the two-week payer test passes.
result.pitch:
When a residential solar installer fails, the loans on its half-built jobs stay on someone's books. A credit union that funded 39 loans of $30-35k up front, as Tucson's Old Pueblo CU did, holds more than $1M of exposure on roofs producing nothing, with borrowers pausing payments and nobody on staff who knows what a contractor-of-record transfer is. The big captives (GoodLeap, Sunrun, the other Freedom Forever financiers) have court authority, systems access and in-house project staff, so we do not sell to them. We sell to holders with none.

The product is a cure desk, not a crew. Within days of a closure we find affected lenders and offer a 10-business-day Triage Sprint: for each loan, pull the public permit and utility record, screen for liens and estate-held hardware, and return a tier (paperwork-only, inspection fix, missing hardware, unwind) with a cost range and a cure-or-unwind call. Unwind is a valid answer; telling a lender which jobs not to fund is part of the value. Jobs worth curing go to a licensed contractor-of-record partner who holds the license, insurance and contract. We manage the file for a flat fee against lender-issued purchase orders and a deposit, so we never front labor, permit fees or hardware.

result.title: Exclusivity-Stage Data Audit for China-Origin Preclinical Assets
result.one_liner: A fixed-price, 10-day written red-flag audit of a China-origin preclinical package, sold at exclusivity to biotechs and NewCo platforms with no China bench and delivered from outside China by a named FDA-experienced bilingual principal. It is a capped practice with a ceiling near $0.2-0.9M a year, not a venture.
result.pitch: Honest framing first: this is a capped audit practice, not a venture. When a mid-cap biotech or NewCo platform with no China bench reaches exclusivity on a China-origin preclinical asset, it is about to commit tens of millions on a data package it cannot read and a sponsor's assurance it cannot test. The Exclusivity-Stage Data Audit sells that buyer a fixed-price, 10-business-day written red-flag audit at the one moment a budget exists: after term sheet, before definitive agreement. A named, FDA-experienced, Mandarin-fluent principal and contractor scientists use bought machine translation and extraction to read the study reports. They then check cross-document consistency, GLP and GMP certificate scope, CRO and CDMO inspection records, and Western-format IND gaps, and they quote the rework cost and delay that should move price and milestones. Because sellers control raw data, there is no 72-hour raw-data promise. Stage A works on what the data room and public record show. Buyers' counsel get a standard audit-right clause, so a supervised raw-data audit (Stage B) becomes a contract term and not a favor. Operating rules cut China-side risk: US, EU or Singapore-resident staff only, no PRC presence, seller-consented materials only, no ownership investigations, preclinical and CMC only. Liability is capped, third-party reliance excluded, and every memo lists what was not checked, because paper review cannot catch concealment. Stage A is $45k fixed; Stage B is capped time-and-materials. The serviceable pool is $0.75-1.85M a year, so revenue tops out near $0.2-0.9M. The only reachable moat is earned reputation from a published, timestamped record of red flags that proved right. Gates: a credentialed principal, and at least 4 of 10 buyers naming a $30k-plus budget owner.
result.wedge_customer: A first- or second-time China in-licensor with no China-based staff, at exclusivity or term-sheet stage on a preclinical asset with roughly $20M+ upfront. One named person (BD/corp-dev head, CSO, or the NewCo sponsor's partner) owns a per-deal external-expense budget. Examples to test, not claims they would buy: K2 Therapeutics-type NewCo vehicles, mid-cap biotechs with one or two China in-licenses, and royalty funds opening Asia desks. Excluded on purpose: Novartis-type in-house teams, RA Swiftbridge, Banyan, and bankers as a channel.
result.first_product: Stage A, Package Red-Flag Audit, 10 business days from data-room access. It covers LLM-assisted translation and extraction (bought, not built), cross-document consistency, GLP/GMP certificate scope, public CRO/CDMO inspection history, licensed list lookups, and a Western-format IND-readiness gap list with estimated rework cost and months. The memo always includes a "not checked" section. Stage B, Confirmatory Data Audit, is triggered by a standard audit-right clause kit that buyers' counsel insert into the term sheet or definitive agreement, giving a named auditor a supervised raw-data and audit-trail review of a defined sample of studies. Preclinical and CMC only at launch. Out of scope: 72-hour promises, an inspection database, a BIOSECURE mapping product, on-the-ground collection in China, and human-genetic-resource or clinical raw data.
result.pricing: Stage A is $45k fixed (range $40-55k by package size). The first two founding clients pay $35k in exchange for anonymized case-study rights. There are no $20k pilots, because they lose money and test the wrong price. Stage B is capped time-and-materials of $25-60k, only if the audit right is in the contract. No retainers in year 1; a pre-negotiated framework agreement is offered after two engagements. Delivery cost is $18-30k per Stage A [inference], giving a 33-60% contribution margin at $45k. Do not sell below $40k except to the two founding clients. Contractors only; no hires until backlog exceeds about 3 months. The payer is the buyer's per-deal external-expense budget; this is unproven and is the core of the test.
result.why_now: Rebuilt, and BIOSECURE is dropped. (1) Stakes per deal rose: Western-China licensing deals went from 42 in 2022 to 93 in 2025 (Evaluate), and average upfronts rose from $52M to $172M (Evaluate) or $38.8M to $77.7M (Reuters definition). (2) FDA is raising the cost of unverifiable packages: Goodwin (Sep 2026) reports more BIMO inspections including foreign Phase 1 and public flagging of sites that deny access. No FDA refusal of China preclinical data is documented yet, so this is partly rhetorical. (3) LLM translation and extraction became a commodity, so a small shop can read a Chinese-language package in days. This also helps competitors. The 18 Dec 2026 BIOSECURE list is a date, not a spend event. This would not have worked in 2019, when deal flow was a fraction of today's.
result.moat: No durable power at launch, stated plainly. Scale, network and switching costs are absent. A cornered resource fails because Novartis is hiring the same bilingual profile. The reachable power is Branding, at 18-30 months. The mechanism is a hash-timestamped log of red flags, with anonymized aggregate hit rates published by category, plus public retrospective case memos. Competitors found do not publish falsifiable calibration. A secondary, partial counter-positioning applies only against large vendors (ICON, Deloitte, PwC), who cannot sell $45k fixed-fee work without cannibalizing hourly engagements; boutiques like Vision and Alacrita can copy freely. This is a 2-4 year window harvest, so keep costs variable and run for cash, not growth.
result.bottom_up_market: The 2026 run rate is about 170-190 China out-licensing deals (H1: 81 by NMPA, 86 by Insight). Removing big pharma (about 40% of assets in-licensed, IQVIA via Fierce) and deals with no verifiable package leaves 85-110 addressable transactions a year [dossier assumption]. At exclusivity, 15-25% attach [no source] gives 13-28 Stage A engagements at $45k, or $0.6-1.3M. Stage B follow-on at 30-50% of those, about $40k each, adds $0.15-0.55M. The serviceable pool is $0.75-1.85M a year. Capturable share at maturity is 25-50%, so revenue is roughly $0.2-0.9M a year. The dossier's $1.5-4M included retainers and a BIOSECURE product that are now removed. The 85-110 and 15-25% figures are replaced by counts and purchase history in the 2-week test.
result.competitors_and_edge: Direct on paper: Vision Lifesciences (data-integrity and GCP audit-trail spot checks, CMC tech-transfer audit; no price, customers or credentials found; priced as retainer plus success fee), Alacrita (framework agreements and "DD Readiness"), and ICON (technical DD with an APAC-licensor case). Overlapping: Parexel, Deloitte China, PwC, BiotechGo, and Dark Horse Consulting China (Shanghai office opened 10 Sep 2026). AI and data inputs: Patsnap, Perceptic, Prudentia, Redica, Kharon, Sayari; these are bought, not competed with. In-house substitutes: Novartis, RA Swiftbridge, Banyan. The "GAP" label is withdrawn. Claimed edge, none proven: a named principal with red flags that proved right; fixed price and time at the stage that has a budget; a contract clause kit that creates its own Stage B demand; a published calibration record; and zero China nexus. Vision's Shanghai and Hong Kong presence is ground truth I give up. If buyers already get this from Vision, Alacrita or ICON at similar price and speed, the idea is dead.
result.riskiest_assumption: A first- or second-time China in-licensor at exclusivity, with a named budget owner, will pay $35-45k to a vendor with no track record for a preclinical data audit. The alternative is relying on the sponsor, a banker, in-house generalists, or an established vendor. There is no direct willingness-to-pay evidence: no price list, RFP or budget line was found. A second gate is that a credentialed, FDA-experienced bilingual principal exists and will be named.
result.two_week_test: Fourteen days, under $300, about 30 founder hours. (1) Days 1-3: census the licensees in Western-China deals from 2025 to H1 2026 from public announcements and trackers. Tag China office and prior China in-licenses, and count the no-bench, first- or second-time buyers with a named BD owner. (2) Days 3-14: hold 10-12 purchase-history interviews, from about 150 targeted outreach messages. Ask what verification they did on the last China deal, who did it, what it cost, who approved it and from which budget, and whether their counsel would insert an audit-right clause. Close by asking for a $45k engagement and a one-paragraph written statement of intent. (3) Days 1-10: screen 5 ex-pharma bilingual GLP-tox/CMC-regulatory scientists for a willing, named principal. (4) Learn competitor quotes from buyers; do not pose as a buyer. Go if 4 or more of 10 name a budget owner and a figure of $30k or more, at least 2 bought outside technical verification in the last 12 months from a non-bank, non-law firm, at least 2 sign an intent statement, and at least 1 principal candidate agrees to be named. Extend and run 10 more calls if 2-3 of 10 give a number. Kill if 1 or fewer do, or if most say the sponsor, a bank or an in-house person handles it, or demand big-brand reliance. Fewer than 8 completed calls is inconclusive, not a pass. After a Go: PRC counsel opinion, an E&O quote and a capped engagement letter come first, then three paid engagements of $35k or more within 90 days of selling (at least two not law-firm-sourced), else kill.
result.how_critiques_were_addressed:
Accepted: top-tier buyers are excluded (Novartis, RA, Banyan do it in house), and the "white space" claim is withdrawn (Vision, Alacrita and ICON all sell versions). The 72-hour sprint, database, BIOSECURE mapping product, $20k pilot and BIOSECURE why-now are dropped.
Changed wedge and stage: the buyer is a first- or second-time, no-bench licensee, sold only at exclusivity so a budget exists. Triage is never sold, which answers the funnel critique that 50-100 early screens exist for each closed deal.
Data access: Stage A uses only what is given plus public record, and Stage B is a standard contract clause so asking does not signal distrust. Preclinical and CMC only, to avoid human-data rules. Open item: whether remote viewing counts as a transfer under CAC rules, which PRC counsel must answer.
China-side legal risk: no PRC presence or staff, seller-consented materials only, no ownership investigations, and a PRC counsel gate.
Liability: capped, non-reliance, E&O launch gate, an explicit "not checked" section, and no claim to catch concealment. If buyers need big-brand blame transfer, the product loses; the interviews count them.
Channel: no referral fees, no exclusivity, a 30% revenue cap per firm, privilege demoted, bankers not a channel.
Economics: $45k fixed with a $40k floor, contractors only, a 33-60% margin that must be validated.
Moat: Branding only, through a published calibration record, plus partial counter-positioning against large vendors; no durable power, so it is run for cash over a 2-4 year window.
Not refuted, only testable: willingness to pay, budget owner, segment size and the policy band. The ceiling is $0.2-0.9M a year, and it needs a credentialed principal, so it is dead as a venture and alive only as a capped practice.

result.title: Operating Authority Memos for Data Center Lenders
result.one_liner: An attorney-signed, white-label memo for lender technical advisors and project-finance counsel that maps each grid-curtailment trigger to the legal authority governing a data center campus's backup generators. It is not a company on current evidence.
result.pitch:
Power-risk diligence for data center lenders has one unpriced corner: what a campus may legally do with its on-site generators when the grid curtails it for reasons that are not a declared emergency. In declared emergencies the answer is mostly "run them". FPA 202(c)(3) shields compliance with DOE orders, and Texas SB 2321 lets TCEQ waive hours-of-operation enforcement. But PJM's IRAS (filed Aug 2026, start June 1, 2027 if FERC approves) would curtail new 50 MW+ loads before an emergency, and ERCOT is still writing its large-load rules. In those market-triggered events the air permit and 40 CFR 63.6640(f) still bind. Nobody independent has mapped, campus by campus, which curtailment triggers fall under which legal authority.

We sell an attorney-signed Operating Authority Memo. It has a permit inventory with remaining headroom, a trigger-by-trigger authority matrix, and an hours-exposure range taken from published studies. The price is $12-20k and delivery takes five business days. It is sold white-label to lender technical advisors and project-finance counsel on unrated or spec PJM and ERCOT financings. They already own the diligence and the reliance paper. A licensed air attorney is engaged by them, not by us. There is no cost-to-cure cross-sell and no subscription until a lender writes the condition.

This is not a venture-scale company. Without a lender mandate it is a $15-280k a year side practice, and with one the dossier's $1.5-6M mature case applies. The next two weeks decide whether anyone with budget has ever put this on a checklist, and I put the odds of a pass below 10%.
result.wedge_customer: Lender-side technical advisors (Salute, TBH, Sargent & Lundy, Ankura type) and project-finance lender counsel on unrated, spec and neocloud financings of new 50 MW+ PJM or ERCOT campuses. They buy white-label. The borrower pays through the lender's third-party report budget. Hyperscaler-tenant deals, campuses on behind-the-meter gas or batteries, and direct sales to credit committees are out of scope.
result.first_product: Operating Authority Memo: 6-10 pages in 5 business days, signed by an independent air attorney engaged by the buyer. It contains a permit inventory (per-engine and pooled caps, tier, permitted uses, headroom) and a trigger-tier matrix. Tier A is a DOE 202(c) order, Tier B is an ERCOT emergency with TCEQ discretion, Tier C is market-triggered non-emergency curtailment, and Tier D is baseline testing hours. It also gives a Tier C hours-exposure range taken only from published studies. The cost-to-cure section, the permit-modification cross-sell, subscriptions and alerts are removed.
result.pricing: $12-20k per memo, quoted at $15k from the first conversation, with no free reports because free reports measure appetite for free work. Refresh at $4-6k only if a lender writes surveillance into a covenant, and it is modeled at zero until then. Portfolio subscriptions are dropped. The original $20-45k is withdrawn because white-label buyers will push price down. Estimated gross margin is 20-80%, central about 55%, and near zero on the first five memos.
result.why_now: The enabling change is real but its date is later than pitched. PJM's IRAS (ER26-3515, filed 2026-08-13) would curtail new 50 MW+ loads from 2027-06-01. PJM's Large Load Registry will collect backup-generation permitting limits. Texas SB 6 requires disclosure from 75 MW+ loads. It would not have worked in 2019, so the timing is real. But FERC had no known IRAS order, the companion backstop procurement is suspended to Feb 28, 2027, and Texas permitting is paused pending the ERCOT audit (about December 2026). Realistic revenue starts H2 2027 to 2028, after 12-18 months of waiting on a rule that may not take effect as drafted.
result.moat: No Power is reachable in the first 18 months. Counter-positioning is conditional and unverified: if LTA E&O carriers will not let them opine on air-permit interpretation, they must subcontract it. That is testable with one question. Cornered resource is weak: it is an engaged air attorney with E&O who will sign, plus a corpus of attorney-reviewed tier interpretations by state, which becomes process power only after about 30 memos. The licensed attorney or firm captures that moat, so a non-lawyer founder is a vendor to it.
result.bottom_up_market: 15-55 PJM/ERCOT closings a year where the lender carries power risk (dossier; the underlying financing count is a vendor tracker of 41 in 2025 and 50 in 2026 through Oct 10, plus an assumed 1-2x for private loans). Haircut 1: 30-50% are IRAS-exposed or rely on diesel rather than gas or batteries (assumed), giving about 5-28. Haircut 2: 25-50% buy rather than absorb in-house absent a mandate (assumed), giving about 1-14 memos a year. At $12-20k that is about $15k-$280k a year without a mandate. With a lender mandate and covenants the dossier's $1.5-6M mature case applies, but nobody has shown the mandate exists. This is a boutique practice, not a $10M company.
result.competitors_and_edge: Closest: lender technical advisors (Salute's LTA phase 2 already includes a permits check; TBH, Sargent & Lundy, Ankura), lender counsel (Davis Polk, Ropes & Gray), air-permit consultancies (Trinity), and funded adjacent substitutes. Those are Azraq (AI lender risk platform, pre-seed July 2026), GridCARE ($64M Series A), Emerald AI (load flexibility) and Parametrix (parametric SLA insurance). The edge is a service edge, not a technology edge: a five-day, fixed-price, attorney-signed tier matrix for deals where the LTA has no air-law bench. It is sold to the incumbents as a subcontract, not against them. The dataset and independence claims are retracted. Phase I is also borrower-paid, and permit files are bespoke and mostly public.
result.riskiest_assumption: A person who controls spend or conditions on at least one live or upcoming PJM/ERCOT financing treats generator-hour exposure under non-emergency curtailment as a felt, priced credit question, and will request a quote of $12k or more or write it into a checklist. If it is only a footnote settled by "DOE 202(c) will cover it", there is no business. A secondary assumption is that Tier C survives legal scrutiny.
result.two_week_test: Oct 14-27, 2026, under about $1,500 cash. Days 1-2: write a one-page scope, a redacted sample tier matrix from one public campus permit, and a $15k, 5-day quote, with no free offer. Days 2-12: contact 25 LTA/engineer staff, project-finance counsel and debt originators to get 5-8 real conversations. Ask whether generator-hour analysis has ever appeared on a closing checklist and who paid, whether they would want it if FERC approves IRAS and from whose budget, whether their E&O allows permit-law opinions or they would subcontract, and whether they would accept an SOW at $15k. In parallel, pay an independent air attorney for one hour on whether IRAS or ERCOT-directed generator use is non-emergency and outside 202(c)(3) and EPA's Jan 2026 guidance. Pre-registered pass: at least one written SOW, NDA or quote request at $12k or more on a named live deal, or at least two independent confirmations that the item was on a real closing checklist in the last 12 months, and the attorney confirms Tier C is real. Kill: no written request, at most one prior-checklist instance, or the attorney says it is emergency or 202(c)-covered. "Interesting" and "send me a sample" count as failures. Fewer than five conversations is inconclusive, not a pass.
